maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I was giving a review of Canada's trade position, and I shall now complete that review. I had covered the situation with regard to our relations with the commonwealth, the trade blocs in Europe and the United States. I have left to consider our relationships with other areas of the world such as Latin America, Japan and Russia, about which I will say a few words.
In so far as Latin America is concerned, that area continued to face serious economic difficulties from May of last year until the present, mainly as a result of low world prices in most of the primary commodities which are the major source of their export earnings. They have been making some progress toward the establishment of regional trading groups. At a meeting held in Panama in May of last year, all 20 Latin American republics discussed a draft plan for a free trade arrangement covering the Latin American area. No substantial measure of agreement was reached.

Later in 1959 conferences were held at Lima and Montevideo by a smaller group of countries with a view to establishing a southern free trade area as an initial step. On February 18 of this year seven countries, Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Mexico, Paraguay, Peru and Uruguay signed a treaty establishing a Latin America free trade association. This treaty provides for the gradual elimination over a period of 12 years of customs tariffs and quantitative restrictions on essential trade between the member countries.
In the field of economic regionalism, about which we have been talking, the Central American free trade treaty came into force in June, 1959 for an initial period of 10 years on being ratified by Guatemala, El Salvador and Nicaragua. Costa Rica and Honduras have indicated a willingness to accede to that treaty.
From the point of view of Canadian trade interests, the establishment of the Latin American free trade association, with a population of 140 million, could in the long run provide an expanding market for Canadian products. In discussing this subject at the fifteenth session of GATT the Canadian delegation stressed that the free trade association should be outward looking, and that their plans should lead to an expansion and not a diversion of trade.
Canadian sales to Latin American countries declined slightly in 1959, but toward the end of the year began to show a firmer trend. Where noticeable decreases did occur, as in sales to Brazil and Mexico, the decline was over a number of products and resulted from intensified restrictions on imports rather than actual loss of markets. Brazil, for example, bought less newsprint, railway rails, aluminum, electrical apparatus and zinc. Mexico reduced its purchases of aluminum very sharply, and of pulp and primary iron and steel more moderately. The marked gain in sales to Colombia represented an increase in exports of wheat grain from Canada; sales of wheat to Ecuador also rose by $1 million. Venezuela, now Canada's largest market in Latin America, increased wheat purchases but sharply reduced those of wheat flour due to the establishment of new domestic capacity. Milk, egg and dairy product sales continued to increase, as did those of iron and steel goods and synthetic resins.
A major portion of Canada's imports from Latin America consists of crude petroleum from Venezuela. As a result of the expanding use of Canadian crude, these purchases continued to decline. Other imports remained quite stable in 1959, lower coffee prices being offset by a larger volume of purchases. Of

other major items, raw sugar imports from Cuba declined, while cotton purchases in Mexico rose from 1958 levels.
In total, Canada's exports to Latin America in 1958 were valued at $180 million, and at $173 million in 1959. Our imports from that region in 1958 were valued at $380 million, and an estimate for 1959 of about $345 million, so the balance of trade is in favour of Latin America.
I wish to say just a word with regard to our trade with Japan, of which quite a bit has been said recently and commented upon in the papers across the country. The Japanese economy was prosperous in 1959. There was a steady rise of Japanese imports, exports and reserves of foreign exchange. Canada's export trade responded to these influences, rising from about $105 million in 1958 to about $140 million last year. Wheat and flour sales figured prominently in this increase, rising from $64 million in 1958 to $71 million in 1959. Japan has become our second largest importer of Canadian wheat, alternating that position with Germany from year to year.
This is a very important market for Canadian wheat and flour. Other agricultural exports showing improvement were flax seed and rapeseed. In industrial materials, export increases in a wide range of commodities reflected the increased industrial production in Japan. Exports of sulphate pulp, iron ore, asbestos, aluminum and copper rose substantially; those of zinc and chemicals, more moderately.
Canadian imports from Japan also rose very rapidly in 1959 to an estimated $105 million, from the 1958 value of $70 million. Textiles are the leading imports from Japan. The rise, in addition, was spread over a large range of light consumer goods such as boot and shoes, sewing machines, cameras and photographic equipment, hand tools and toys and hardwood plywoods. In January of this year our exports to Japan were valued at $9.1 million as compared with $7.6 million, in January, 1959.
The Leader of the Opposition discussed the Soviet trading bloc and the threat to the western world in the trading sphere of that area, and this question has been the subject of comment by various people from time to time. The Soviet union has been participating in international trade to an increasing extent. While the bulk of her trade continues to be with the Soviet bloc, exports to and imports from western countries have also expanded.
Canada has been participating in this trade to some limited degree. In the 1956 trade agreement between Canada and the U.S.S.R.
Trade Balance
the Soviets undertook to purchase 400,000 tons of Canadian wheat valued at approximately $25 million in each of the three years of the agreement. In 1959, following expiration of this agreement, Canadian exports to Russia declined to $12,740,000. Direct imports from the Soviet union into Canada for the first 11 months of 1959 amounted to $2,258,000. As I have mentioned on many occasions, negotiations are still continuing between Canada and Russia and we are looking toward a renewal of the trade agreement.
Although there may be some dangers in Soviet participation in international trade, there are also opportunities for Canada. However, we have to realize that in many respects Canada's resources are similar to those of Russia, particularly forest products, nonferrous metals, and grains; and if the U.S.S.R. should engage in disruptive selling practices, Canadian export interests could be seriously affected. But it is not reasonable to conclude that in every instance in which Canadian exports may be meeting Soviet competition, unfair trading practices are involved. We are aware of the dangers there may be in trade as it is conducted by members of the Soviet bloc, and we are aware of the need to safeguard the Canadian economy from any disturbance which might arise.
Our trade with the communist bloc countries on the export side consists mainly of wheat and barley, which fluctuates widely in amount and destination from year to year as local conditions dictate. Russia purchased slightly less wheat in 1959, and virtually no barley, against 5 million bushels in 1958. Communist China bought no grains in 1959 but small amounts of copper, nickel, drugs and chemicals. Poland, on the other hand, re-entered the market for both barley-5 million bushels-and wheat-6 million bushels. Imports from these countries amounted to $15 million in 1958. These were largely composed of edible nuts, some types of textiles and brushes from communist China and a wide range of consumer goods from Czechoslovakia.
Looked at in detail, Canadian exports to the Sino-Soviet bloc were $30.3 million in 1958 and $33.8 million in 1959. Imports in 1958 amounted to $15.1 million, and the estimate for 1959 is close to that figure. Thus the balance in this trade has been in our favour, although it is not extensive.
Mr. Speaker, that completes what I have to say with regard to the various regions with which our trade has been conducted. Before I conclude I should like to refer to the amendment which was introduced by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson).

Trade Balance

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext: Hardly worth mentioning, is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext: The Minister of Justice says it is hardly worth mentioning, and that expresses my opinion precisely.

maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext: Then why talk for three hours?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext:
Because, unfortunately, it is a negative amendment. There is no constructive attitude taken in this amendment. It expresses grave concern. It starts off on a gloomy note. It talks about the deterioration of Canada's trading position, yet Canada's trading position has not deteriorated over the last three years; it has vastly improved. So the amendment is inaccurate in its phrasing.
Then, of course, it is inaccurate in that it lumps together the invisible items, those items which were mentioned last night concerning freight and service charges, tourist expenditure, interest and dividends on foreign investments in this country; the amendment lumped all these together with the deficit in commodity trade, thereby distorting the picture.
Then the resolution goes on to urge the government to deal with this serious problem, as it is called, by taking effective action. I showed last night that we were taking effective action and that we have been taking effective action during the last two and a half a years.
The amendment ends by suggesting the working out of proposals for the establishment, on a gradual and progressive basis, of an Atlantic free trade area. That is a typical sentence coming from the Leader of the Opposition; inconclusive, vague and difficult to pin down. Of course when the Leader of the Opposition was talking about this he said he knew these things could not be done very quickly and that we would have to move cautiously; that it would be a gradual adjustment over a period of years, and so on.
Four years ago in this House of Commons a debate on Canada's trading position took place. We were then on the opposition side. It is interesting to look back at the amendment we put forward dealing with a situation something like this; only then, in 1956, the deficit trade balance was double what it is on this occasion. But our amendment was constructive. It was subsequently embodied in the policy for our party which received the approbation of the Canadian people in 1957 and 1958.
Our amendment in those circumstances, instead of starting off in a gloomy way, was

constructive. It was constructive, and it advocated a national policy to develop our national resources for the benefit of all parts of Canada. It went on to stress the importance of developments in Canadian life rather than simply dwelling on the gloomy side and attempting to paint a picture of concern and dismay for the Canadian people.
That is one of the basic differences between the Liberal party and the Conservative party. The Conservative party from the time of confederation has been the party of progress, the party of development in this country, and the Liberal party has been the party of little Canadianism, as I expressed it last year, the party of the small view, the gloomy attitude, the party of despondent characterization.

maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext: C. D. Howe, for example.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext: It gives no inspiration to the Canadian people. In this particular instance, when Canadian trade is in a flourishing condition-*

maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext: Hence our $1J billion deficit.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext:
-and the economy is growing and when, as indicated by the reports from the premiers there is in every province of Canada a feeling of optimism, it is under these conditions that the Leader of the Opposition introduces his gloom and despondency and plays Canada down.
I reaffirm what I said yesterday, that Canada has a well defined and positive trade policy which is practical and dynamic. Its objective is the furtherance of Canada's export trade in all the markets of the world, be they national or regional. Our policy comprises both our trade relations which provide the framework for the expansion of trade, and our trade promotional activities which comprise the many and different ways in which the Department of Trade and Commerce assists our exporters to find and take advantage of market opportunities abroad.
There are eight facets to our program, which may be listed as follows: (1) trade negotiations (2) trade conferences and (3) trade treaties. These are all in the realm of international relations in which we hare been particularly active.

maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext: Especially with Russia.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext:
To continue; (4) trade promotion, (5) trade fairs, (6) trade financing, (7) trade missions and (8) trade publicity.
Under those eight points we have the fields of activity in which the Department of Trade and Commerce is involved. In the field of trade relations our policy has been through trade negotiations, through trade conferences and through the treaties which have been

entered into with our trading partners to improve Canada's access to foreign markets.
We have been endeavouring with a great measure of success to reduce both the tariff and non-tariff barriers to trade which have faced Canadian exports in the post-war period. As a result of multilateral tariff negotiations the tariffs facing Canada in the United States and other markets have been considerably reduced, and Canada will be taking part in the next round of such negotiations scheduled to commence at the end of this year.
With regard to non-tariff barriers, the very substantial reduction in quantitative restrictions on trade throughout the world and the virtual elimination of discrimination against dollar exports are a striking illustration both of the improved financial position of our trading partners and of the success which has attended our persistent efforts to do away with these temporary and artificial barriers to our trade.
I have indicated the measures we have taken in the face of the development of regional trading blocs in Europe and elsewhere. Our efforts have been directed and continue to be directed to ensuring that these regional groups have an expansionary rather than a restrictive effect on world trade and in particular on Canadian exports.
As the house knows, Canada is actively engaged in discussions with the European countries and with the United States concerning certain of the problems to which the formation of the European economic community and the European free trade area give rise. That is the Six and the Seven. In these discussions we are taking the necessary action to safeguard and further our trade interests. The house may rest assured that our approach to the new problems in the trade policy field, including the question of trade relations with regional economic groupings, is under the most active consideration, and that our policy is to serve Canadian interest in accordance with the requirements of changing world circumstances.
Our policy of assistance to Canadian exporters involves trade promotion in all its aspects. Throughout the world, and in all markets of significance to Canada, we have trade commissioners on the ground whose function is to seek out and promote Canadian trade. In this regard Canadian exporters are served as well as or better than those of any country in the world. This is not to suggest, of course, that there is no room for improvement. What we must do constantly is adjust ourselves to meet the challenges of changing world trade. The contacts I have with the Canadian business community suggest to me
Trade Balance
that our exporters are well satisfied with the work of the Canadian trade commissioner service.

maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext: Especially in the uranium industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext:
Scarcely a month goes by that I do not receive letters from Canadian businessmen who have been abroad reporting to me that they have been very courteously and ably served by our trade commissioners whom they have met. The trade promotional activities of our trade commissioners are supplemented by our participation in trade fairs and by the dispatch from Canada of trade missions.
The Department of Trade and Commerce is active in stimulating the interest of Canadian exporters in these special and worth-while activities. It is part of the department's program to step up the number of trade missions from Canada, and we are developing new and more flexible techniques for this aspect of our trade promotion.
With regard to trade fairs, our program for 1960 is interesting and extensive and I should like to give the house some idea of its scope. There are approximately 28 large fairs or exhibitions in which Canada will be participating this year. The Department of Trade and Commerce through its exhibition branch makes arrangements at these trade fairs for Canadian businessmen to display their goods.
Let me cite a few examples. The ideal home exhibition in London, England which is proceeding at this time is, as far as Canada is concerned, largely devoted to the presentation of food products and consumer goods. There is on display there a special house constructed from Canadian lumber and sponsored by the British Columbia lumbermen's association and by the dominion government. Canadian firms will be exhibiting in the Rand easter show in Johannesburg in the month of April. There will be a presentation of engineering products, farm implements, forest products and furs. At the Milan fur show in March there will be a display of fur pelts and fur garments. A similar fair will be held in Paris in April at which there will be a display of Canadian fur pelts and garments.
In January of this year we participated in the national association of home builders convention in Chicago at which there was a presentation of woods used in home construction. We also participated in the national sporting goods show at Chicago early in February. We will be taking part in an exhibition in New York dealing with the equipment used in atomic industry. In Detroit in April we will participate in a presentation of engineering tools at the American society

of tool engineering show. At the Frankfurt, Germany fur fair in April we will display fur pelts and garments. In New York in May we will participate in the design engineering show. In Leeds, England we will take part in the building trades exhibition at which building materials will be displayed. We will also participate in the international specialty food and confection show at Chicago in June, and at the St. Erik's fair in Stockholm in September at which there will be a presentation of industrial and consumer goods. This is the second year in which we are participating in that fair. I had the pleasure of seeing the exhibits last year, and they were very good and should be quite a stimulus to Canadian trade.
In September Canadians will be showing their products at the British food fair in London. In October there will be a showing of wood and building materials at the Manchester building trades fair. In Philadelphia, in October, we will be participating in the forty second metal congress and exhibition, where industrial machinery and materials will be shown. At Amsterdam in May of this year there will be a bakery exhibition at which Canadian wheat and flour will be exhibited, and so it goes, we are also represented at trade fairs and exhibits in various other places throughout the world, including some of the eastern European countries. There is a fair in Poland in June, one in Yugoslavia in September, and so on. I have not given the entire list, but those I have given will give the house an idea of some of the activity that is being carried on by the exhibition branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce with the co-operation of Canadian businessmen.
With respect to the financing of trade, the house is well aware of the facilities in Canada for export credits insurance and of the amendments made last session to the Export Credits Insurance Act. In the department we are watching carefully the credit facilities available in other countries, with a view to ensuring that within our means, and in accordance with the realistic requirements of trade, Canadian exporters are not placed at an unfair disadvantage in world trade. We have found that many of the exporting countries are making credit facilities available to their exporters, some of them along the lines that we do in the Export Credits Insurance Act.
In the field of trade publicity we are constantly bringing to the attention of the Canadian business community the opportunities of trade which exist abroad, and through our trade commissioner service and in other ways we bring the availability of Canadian goods

to the attention of foreign importers. In all these activities the Department of Trade and Commerce is endeavouring to serve the interests of the Canadian exporter, and the orientation of these activities is being constantly adjusted to the developing requirements of foreign markets.
The expansion of our export sales cannot be brought about just by the Department of Trade and Commerce alone; we have to have, and we do get, the active co-operation of the business community. Canadian businessmen are addressing themselves vigorously to the problem of selling in what has become a highly competitive world. The years when an easy sellers' market existed are over. New techniques and new initiative will be required if we are to exploit the opportunities which exist, but I am confident that Canadians will rise to meet the challenges which face us in the export markets, and the Department of Trade and Commerce will do all in its power to assist.
Notwithstanding some of the difficulties we face, I am confident that 1960 will show another good year for Canadian trade, with exports exceeding the record level of $5 billion achieved in 1959.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if we had thought that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) was in earnest yesterday afternoon, we might have believed that he was really in a spot when he said that he was taken a bit by surprise by the introduction of an amendment by the Leader of Opposition (Mr. Pearson). Yes, he said, he was facing a problem, and every time the house went into a supply motion, the ministers had to go through a guessing game from week to week as to what the opposition might bring forward.
For a moment last evening, I was tempted to sympathize with him, but after glancing at the northwest gallery, where a host of distinguished departmental officials were gathered, and later on as I listened to that recital of statistics and quotations from reports of all kinds, I soon realized that the minister had not been in earnest and had only been jesting.
I understood that he had been listening to the radio on Sunday and Monday and that he was steeled for the fray.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, the minister said he was in a spot and yet held forth for more than three hours. What would have happened if he had been forewarned? What would

have happened if, charitably, we had let him know we would introduce that amendment? We probably would have heard one of the longest speeches ever delivered in this house.
Mr. Speaker, our foreign trade, the balance of our international payments and the general condition of our economy are outlined in detail in the latest annual report of the Bank of Canada. In fact, that report reveals a few rather disquieting things that call for serious consideration.
In the last five years, we have bought from abroad all kinds of goods, for a total amount of $38.3 billion and we have gained, in exports and other values, the total of $32.2 billion. In other words our deficit over that five-year period is about $6 billion.
Last year our quotas abroad, including investments of non-residents and other debit accounts, have increased by $2.3 billion, which means that our gross international debt, at the end of 1959, reached another all-time high of $24 billion.
The net Canadian international debt now amounts to $15.4 billion, twice as much as at the end of 1955, and $3.5 billion more than at the end of 1957.
The current accounts' deficit in goods and other services reached $1.46 billion in 1959, the highest we ever had.
The deficit in the invisible trade alone- that is in transactions relating to services of all kinds and to transfers of interest and dividends-was $1,074 million for the year just ended or twice as high as it was in 1955, and naturally that is another record.
Our exports of goods increased in 1959, but on the other hand, imports were much greater than in 1958, with the result that the trade deficit at the end of 1959 was $386 million. While our current account deficit with the United States for merchandise and other services is slightly lower than in 1956 and 1957, it still amounts to $1,236 million.
Our favourable trade balance with the United Kingdom and the other countries of the sterling area, which reached $502 million in 1952, is now down to $64 million as of the end of 1959.
For the first time in 1959 our trade balance with the other European countries, the O.E.E.C. countries, not counting the United Kingdom, has fallen from a usually favourable position to a deficit of $149 million, and finally
Trade Balance
our surplus with other countries also shows deficits, more specifically a deficit of $139 million in 1959.
Given a little more time, Mr. Speaker, the present government will set all kinds of new records. Indeed, in hardly three years since it took office, this government never stopped piling up new records.
In addition to the two I have just mem-tioned, the government had many other records to its credit, such as: record budget deficits, a sharp rise in the national debt, alltime high interest rates and an extremely disturbing rate of unemployment. Of course, the money situation, too, is extremely tight; so much so that municipal governments, small borrowers and small businessmen, the very people the government should be protecting, have the greatest difficulties in finding the money they need.
As a result of this tight money policy, which the government is pursuing and apparently has no intention of relaxing, provincial and municipal administrations as well as crown corporations, have to go to the United States to borrow hundreds of millions of dollars every year, through bond issues, to get the money they need to maintain current services, and therefore to meet current expenditures, and not capital expenses.
In 1957, such bond issues represented $259 million; in 1958, they rose to $316 million and in 1959, they soared to an all-time high; in other words, provincial governments and municipalities assumed, in the form of loans floated abroad, a mortgage of $473 million. This makes a total of $1 billion 48 million for the last three years, or $100 million more than in the five previous years from 1952 to 1956 inclusive. Here is something which appeared in Le Droit for March 18 in that connection, and I quote:
Since the conversion loan, Ottawa has been monopolizing the Canadian bond market to meet its increased payments.
Payments exclusive of interests.
Provinces therefore are sending their agents to New York for the money they need to cover the necessary cost of roads, hospitals and schools. Even so prosperous a province as Ontario is involved with foreign loans. Urban municipalities are in the same fix because of the sudden increase of their services in respect of hospitals, social welfare and schools.
Those loans by provincial and municipal governments, as well as those granted to other corporations are in American currency and

Trade Balance
must be converted into Canadian dollars. Those operations create an artificial demand for Canadian dollars outside of trade, thus contributing to an increase of the premium and keeping our currency at a rate that is much too high to be beneficial to our economy as a whole.
The gap we are facing now in the balance of our international payments has reached dangerous proportions and can be filled only by a sharp increase in our exports.
Even if our exports have considerably increased since 1952-and I admit they have -the country's present position in respect of international trade is nonetheless not so flourishing as a few years ago. Since 1952, world trade has very rapidly increased, but the part played by Canada today is not what it should be. We have allowed others to take the lead.
Our share of international trade, which had risen from 5.2 to 6.1 per cent between 1951 and 1956, is now back to about 5 per cent, which means a decrease of 1 per cent in the last three years. For several other countries, this trend has worked in the opposite direction. Several countries, among them Germany, Japan, Italy and France have substantially increased their share of world trade.
We are probably the most vulnerable nation with regard to international trade, and that is why we must be very wary in that field. We are vulnerable because we depend to a very great extent on our export trade.
One can easily imagine what would have happened if we had stood our ground. If we had kept our share of world trade, our exports for 1959 would no doubt be ranging about $6 billion instead of $5 billion.
The problem of most concern with regard to the balance of Canada's international payments is undoubtedly the size of our current account deficits in the last few years. The total deficit for the last four years reaches $5,333,000 and naturally, the 1959 deficit of $1,460,000 is an all time high.
Logically, we can close this gap only by increased exports. We can hardly reduce our imports, and there can be no question borrowing to make up for the deficits and to pay interest on the indebtedness already incurred, as well as current expenses, because such loans would merely increase by billions of dollars the cost of living for future generations.

All experts agree that we can and must increase our exports. First of all, we have abundant natural resources; we have the required manpower and technicians, and, what is more important, Canadians have the courage and intelligence necessary to face the situation.
It is time the government made its contribution. So far, all the government has done was to set undesirable records, and that is not the way it will succeed in steadying an increasingly shaky economy. It is being said in many quarters that we are headed for an economic slump. Here is what Le Droit of March 18 last had to say about this:
Unable to establish long term policies, the federal government administers from week to week and lets internal factors determine the economy. It allows expansion to take precedence over production. It lets expenses exceed by $1 billion, at least, the proper level for economic stability. It impassively tolerates excessive imports to be financed, not by funds levied on savings, but by foreign borrowings. Instead of speeding up the decline of inflation, it advocates, in fact if not in principle, an inflation of the money supply and a deficit of expenditures. And one tenth of Canadian manpower stagnates in unemployment.
Our world trade has deteriorated during recent years, there is a danger that this tendency may continue and we must take steps to check it.
The governor of the Bank of Canada proposes certain solutions which can be summed up as follows: we must diversify our production; increase our productivity; put off expenditures which require borrowings, especially from foreign countries; obtain the co-operation of the leaders of the common market and of the free trade area, and finally, do all we can to find new markets. And naturally, the governor of the Bank of Canada adds that we must learn to live within our means, in other words to tighten our belts.
Since the Canadian trade deficit is $1,460 billion, largely due to the size of our merchandise imports, especially from the United States, some people might feel this is a good reason for raising our tariff barriers. Those are the protectionists; there are some in the United States and we have them here too in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, we would be making a big mistake if we tried to reduce our trade deficit through higher tariffs. We cannot afford to million, largely due to the size of our surplus raw materials and for our semifinished products are an absolute necessity.

Our domestic market is much too small to absorb all our mine and forestry products.
The United States are unquestionably our largest market for mining, forest and many other products.
However, the contracts we are able to get there, especially for some of our mining products, are obtainable under conditions imposed by the United States administration, and often as a result of pressures exercised by producers in that country, who consider such restrictions as better protection for their own products.
I would even say that certain United States producers sincerely believe that this is the only answer to this problem. Naturally, this is not the case.
In the light of recent developments- and I mean the cancellation by the United States administration of the options taken by the United States Atomic Energy Board on Canadian production of uranium, in addition to firm purchases which have now been extended beyond 1963-Canada now wishes to be reassured, more than ever, so that important sectors of the Canadian economy be not so unfavourably and seriously affected as was the uranium industry, as a result of certain decisions taken by the United States.
Mr. Speaker, Canadian producers are concerned. They, of course, realize the difficulties we are facing, difficulties resulting from that protectionist policy which prevails among our neighbours to the south. But, Mr. Speaker, their concern goes deeper than that. Canadian producers are wondering whether, actually, the Canadian government is taking the necessary steps to prevent United States government policy from getting even stricter.
Last April, in this house, during the debate on the budget, I asked the same question, saying that we would perhaps have an answer to that question when we knew what attitude the United States government would take with regard to the United States atomic energy board's options on Canadian production of uranium, in addition to firm purchases. We did have that answer in November last, but unfortunately it was a negative one.
We must realize-and that is very important-that many difficulties and problems which are common to us Canadians as well as to our friends the Americans are
Trade Balance
rooted in our trade relations. We must endeavour to smooth them out, or at least lessen them.
We must recognize that our trade relations with our friends the Americans suffered a real set-back when, in 1957, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), in one of his ill-considered statements, said that Canada proposed to divert 15 per cent of our purchases in the United States, in order to increase our imports from the United Kingdom. Fortunately, that statement was not taken seriously. However the threat of diversion had its effects and did not fail to disturb some of our friends to the south.
It might have been pure coincidence, but since this government took over, our mine and oil industries have been subject to restrictions which greatly hamper their expansion and development. Thus, in July 1958, the United States government again applied the U/10 cent per pound tariff on imported copper. We know what that means to Canadian industry.
In October of the same year, the U.S. government decided to apply quotas on imports of lead and zinc. There again, we have an idea of what it can mean to that important Canadian industry. In 1958, our oil industry was affected in the same way. In the latter case, restrictions were taken off, but only partly. As the minister said yesterday, the restrictions were relaxed.
More recently still, in November 1959, it was the uranium industry which received the worst blow. Everybody knows what this means to the affected areas of this country, as well as to our trade balance, as our uranium exports had reached a value of more than $300 million in 1959.
With regard to the decision of the U.S. government, that is the cancellation of options, we do not claim that the Canadian government could exert any pressure on our southern friends to the extent of demanding recognition of every option, but we maintain that Canada could have obtained a much more favourable settlement, and that is the main point.
In yesterday's remarks, especially when he was dealing with our relations and trade with the United States, the minister made a statement which surprised me. After giving us a painstaking report of the rather superficial steps taken by the Canadian government when it approached the U.S. authorities

Trade Balance
to improve our position with regard to the sale of zinc and lead, the minister added, as may be seen on page 2295 of Hansard dated March 21, 1960, and I quote:
Apart from the problem of lead and zinc, Canada's access to United States markets was unaffected by any major adverse developments.
To my mind, the minister was mistaken when he said that. Has he already forgotten the uranium tragedy? I doubt it.
However, we are accusing the government of not having brought to that matter all the attention it deserved.

In 1953, $758 million; in 1954, $594 million; in 1955, $840 million; and in 1956, $1 billion and 283 million. Mr. Speaker, the Conservative government had good cause to worry. I can therefore aptly recall what Mr. James Duncan, of Toronto, used to say: "There is but one step between the loss of economic freedom and that of political freedom".
I read with interest the speech made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). I was really surprised to note that he took inspiration from statements made by Mr. Sharp, the former deputy minister of

trade and commerce, who resigned a few months ago. Yet, the Leader of the Opposition, in my opinion, should not have quoted some of Mr. Sharp's statements, since Mr. Sharp, a former deputy minister, has always been recognized as a political opponent of this government. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the argument of the Leader of the Opposition, based on Mr. Sharp's statements, was valueless, and the same could be said of the arguments of the Leader of the Opposition based on the report of the Bank of Canada.
Everybody knows Mr. Coyne, and is aware of the political statements he made during a previous election campaign. Mr. Coyne has lost the confidence of the people. And I urge the Leader of the Opposition and the members of this house to read the reports of the Bank of Canada from its inception to the present day. You will note that the governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Coyne, did not tell the former government what it should do. In other words, Mr. Coyne indulged in petty politics and mainly lauded government policies. Now that the government has changed, Mr. Coyne wants to dictate his policies to the government. Mr. Coyne has lost the confidence of the people. In my view, this report which he has issued, the Bank of Canada report, is nothing but a cheap political pamphlet. The people's money is being squandered. Mr. Coyne's responsibility is not to dictate to the government, no more than it was to extol the policies of the former government.
The present government enjoys the confidence of the people. This government has just come into power and its policy consists in trying to improve our trade. What did the former government do, a government that was responsible for the loss of our export markets?
Sir, if I were Mr. Coyne, having lost the people's trust, I would resign. Mr. Coyne should resign, because his report is nothing but a cheap political lampoon.
Ladies and gentlemen-Mr. Speaker, because I am speaking here to the Canadian people, I may say "ladies and gentlemen"- from 1950 until 1956, Canada's total commercial deficit increased alarmingly. I have here a table showing the deficit in Canada's trade balance in respect of the rest of the world: in 1951, about $122 million; in 1952, $326 million; in 1953, approximately $210 million; in 1954, about $146 million; in 1955,

about $361 million; and in 1956, approximately $842 million.
Under the former administration, at a time that was referred to as a period of prosperity, our trade balance, which showed a deficit, was not to Canada's advantage. May I say a few words about the improvement in our commercial position in the last few months, after the Conservative government took over. The following figures indicate a lowering of trade tensions in 1957. Until June 1957, there was no appreciable difference. Only during the last six months of 1957 has there been a decrease in the deficit.
Canada's trade deficit with the world at large has decreased under the Conservative administration, from $842 million in 1956 to $693 million in 1957. Canada's trade deficit with the United States has also decreased under the Conservative government, from $1,283 billion in 1956 to $1,064 billion in 1957.

I should like to point out to the house the few steps already taken by the Conservative party to infuse new life into our economic activity. And the present government has fulfilled its promises. We had the commonwealth economic and trade conference. At the time of the 1957 election, the Prime Minister of Canada promised to call an economic and trade conference of commonwealth countries.
At Mont Tremblant, there was no definite agenda prepared by the ministers for the conference, but they decided that the proceedings should deal generally with certain definite matters:
(a)	Importance to all commonwealth countries of changes now taking place in world trade;
(b)	Steps to increase trade between commonwealth countries;
(c)	Progress toward a common objective: greater freedom of trade and payments;
(d)	Degree and trend of economic progress in commonwealth underdeveloped countries and sources of capital and technical assistance to accelerate that progress;
(e)	Economic and trade problems related to agricultural products and other basic products;
(f)	Possibilities, as well as consequences, especially for commonwealth countries, of the European economic community and of the proposed free trade area;
(g)	Provisions for the maintenance, between commonwealth countries, of consultation machinery on economic matters.
A week after having taken office as Prime Minister, the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker, at the commonwealth prime ministers' conference in London, invited the ministers to attend a commonwealth countries' conference in Canada. In September 1957, commonwealth finance ministers met at Mont Tremblant, and I have just outlined the matters which were considered there.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the Canadian trade mission, including fifty delegates, which left Canada for Great Britain, has done much to promote economic activity in Canada. That delegation was headed by the minister of trade (Mr. Churchill! and was composed especially of Canadian industrialists. Its main object was to promote export of United Kingdom products to Canada. I would men-
Trade Balance
tion here, among other things, the benefits that came out of those discussions, because there has been an increase in our salmon and apple exports to the United Kingdom.
Moreover, here is something I find in La Presse for June 25, 1958:
Canada's deficit grows less. At the end of May, it was down to a third of last year's level.
Canada has cut down its trade deficit with the United States, and its total trade deficit to a third of last year's level.
Mr. Speaker, I particularly wish to commend the government for sending a trade mission abroad to publicize our products and to discuss means of increasing our trade.
Unfortunately, the former government did nothing to diversify our export markets. In an article which appeared in La Presse for July 24, under the heading "Foreign trade. We have too many eggs in the same basket", Mr. Laurent Lauzier wrote, and I quote:
On the whole, our foreign trade has made substantial gains since the start of the year. In the first half of 1959, the value of our exports, as reported by the dominion bureau of statistics, has reached a total of $2,416,700,000, as compared to $2,381,300,000 for the first half of 1958. The rise in our foreign sales was particularly sharp in June, reflecting increased merchandise exports to the United States. Last month, our exports to the U.S. rose to $321,100,000, as against $233,600,000 only in June 1958.
In terms of money as well as in volume, our exports made substantial gains which have reduced our trade imbalance and have stimulated industrial activity in some areas of the country.
As a means of expanding our trade, it might be desirable to grant long term credit to purchasers who are likely to become regular customers. I know this method is being adopted by other countries, and surely, it might be considered by Canada.
I also urge the government to keep looking for new markets for our agricultural and industrial products, and to send other trade missions throughout the world.
It might be advisable to send a trade mission to France, and more particularly to the West Indies, to which Canada should turn, because there are great hopes of expanding our trade in that area.
Everyone knows that each year, in every country of the world, there are national or international exhibitions; in fact, there is an international exhibition every year. I strongly urge the Minister of Trade and Commerce to send those countries a bilingual expert who could, at the exhibitions, display the export products of Canada. This would surely be a practical way of telling the world

Trade Balance
about the products Canada can sell on foreign markets.
Everyone knows that Russia and the satellite countries are now launching an economic offensive that might endanger the very foundations of the economy of the western nations. Canadians will have to make sacrifices and people at all levels will have to work hand in hand. Industries will have to avoid raising their prices, and certain unions will have to be careful before asking too high wage increases. In brief, all social classes will have to make sacrifices if we want to continue to export, if we want to compete with the products of Russia and the satellite countries, now making an appearance on the world market at prices that we cannot meet because of the production costs of our own goods.
Mr. Speaker, as a Canadian, I wanted to express my views frankly on international trade, but before closing, perhaps this would be a good time to ask the Leader of the Opposition and his friends not to take too much stock in statements made by friends of the opposition who are recognized opponents of the government. I believe that when they draw their inspiration from statements made by the former deputy minister of trade and commerce, who resigned, their statements are robbed of much of their weight; in fact it destroys their arguments.
I am not sorry for what I said about Mr. Coyne. He is a highly paid employee of the government, and I suggest once again to all the members of this house to read the reports of the Bank of Canada since its foundation. They will notice Mr. Coyne's attitude on this matter.
Once again, I congratulate this government on what it is doing to promote Canada's economy and I strongly urge it to send other trade missions throughout the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we listened last night and again today with great interest to the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill). It was an interesting speech in which he gave a great deal of information to the house but he did not seem at all disturbed about the central problem confronting Canada with regard to its trade position and he was unimpressed by the size of Canada's trade deficit. Indeed, if one can take the word of

the minister, he seems almost pleased that Canada is running this huge trade deficit. The minister has, as a matter of fact, said that the very large deficit in Canada's balance of payments of some $1,460 million is an indication of a rather healthy position in Canada's economy.
As I said, the minister gave us a very interesting discourse for almost three hours. I believe he said when he began his remarks that on a former occasion he complained of not knowing what subject was being advanced in the house for debate. That certainly could not have been the case this time; certainly it was not the case as far as his officials are concerned, because the House of Commons listened very attentively to a rather drab and colourless reading of a whole assortment of uninspiring documents prepared by a number of nameless people in the minister's department. Those statistics perhaps will serve some useful purpose by way of research facilities, but they have very little to do with the questions that have been raised by the opposition in this debate.
Canada's balance of international payments have been worsening steadily for a number of years. In 1954, our deficit on international payments was $432 million. This deficit had been increasing since that time on an annual basis until in 1957 it had reached the high figure of over $1,300 million and is now, as I have already said, the figure that has been referred to a number of times, namely some $1,460 million. What does this mean? It means a tremendous inflow of foreign capital; it means that more and more of Canada's economy and Canadian resources are owned by foreigners and by outside investors.
I think it is perfectly obvious that in an underdeveloped economy, in a country that is looking for and needs outside capital, there is every reason to welcome capital for that development. It also seems to me that in looking for outside capital a nation would be far better advised to receive capital on a long term basis at a fixed interest rate by way of investment in bonds and securities rather than through the great emphasis that is placed today on equity investment. Equity investment in our country means foreign owners are owning a portion of Canadian industry. It is not just a mortgage that is held by foreign investors that we are obliged to meet in the years ahead, but it is a turning over of the ownership of a part of our resources, of a part of our nation, to foreign

investors and as those investments prove lucrative in the days ahead and as profits accumulate they feed upon themselves and they become ever larger and larger so that instead of our nation gradually meeting those foreign obligations and retiring them we are faced with the position where our foreign indebtedness keeps on increasing at an ever more rapid rate. This self-generating process means that our problem is increasing and our difficulties will be multiplied. To meet this argument the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) went back in our investments to 1926. He referred to Canada's gross national product and came to this conclusion, as reported at page 2280 of Hansard:
Consequently, I say that our debt, considered in relation to our wealth producing capacity, is far less of a burden now than it was in the past.
I challenge that statement of the minister; I think it is a wrong statement.
Mr. Pallet!: That statement of the minister is 100 per cent accurate.

speechtext:
I understand my hon. friend is going to make a speech for a change. It will be very pleasant to hear him when he gets up and gives his economic dissertation in attempting to support this very far-reaching and rather fatuous assertion made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. You see, the Minister of Trade and Commerce had to go back to 1926 to find justification for that statement. It would have been interesting if he had made the statement in relation to what has been happening in Canada in the last few years. Our net international indebtedness has been increasing in recent years at a far more rapid rate than has our gross national product. It is not Canada's indebtedness today as compared with 1926 that the argument is about. The argument today is that within recent years there has been an accelerating increase in Canada's foreign obligations and we feel that this will lead to difficult days ahead.
In order to see this picture accurately, it is not enough merely to point out the tremendous increase in Canada's external liabilities. I hold in my hand the dominion bureau of statistics publication, Quarterly Estimates of the Canadian Balance of International Payments, fourth quarter, 1959, and Preliminary Estimates for the Year 1959. On page 14, under "Canadian Liabilities", it lists non-resident owned long term investments in Canada direct, other investments, and these come to a total in 1952 of
Trade Balance
$10.4 billion; in 1954, $12.5 billion; in 1957, $17.5 billion; in 1958, $19.1 billion; and in 1959, a total of $20.6 billion.
If one looks at Canada's net international indebtedness, the figures given on the same page of the same publication for the same year, he finds that Canada's net international indebtedness in 1952 was $5.1 billion; in 1954, $6.8 billion; in 1957, $11.9 billion; in the next year of this administration it went up to $13.5 billion; and in 1959, $15.4 billion. This shows that from 1952 to 1959 there was an increase of $10.3 billion in Canada's net international indebtedness, an increase of some 200 per cent. This demonstrates that the minister misled the house when he said that our debt, considered in relation to our wealth producing capacity, is far less of a burden now than it was in the past. It is less of a burden now than in the extreme past but more of a burden now than five years ago and an increasing burden as this government continues its mismanagement of the affairs of the country.
What are some of the disadvantages of this tremendous inflow of outside capital together with the tremendous increase in Canada's obligations abroad for dividends and profit payments? As I have said, if we were a new economy needing outside capital and if we could get it on a fixed interest basis over a long period of time it would undoubtedly be in the best interests of the country, but as it is now taking place more and more Canadian industries are coming under the control and domination of United States corporations. Canada as a nation and Canadians as citizens of this country are losing control over their economic affairs, over their industries, and in my judgment this endangers the very political existence of our nation as a free and independent nation.
The policies followed in Canada by subsidiaries of outside corporations are often more in the interests of the United States parent company than in Canada's interests. The effect of Canadian law may be jeopardized by an over-all United States law. We have had examples given in the house before. For instance, the Ford Motor Company had an order for the export of 1,000 automobiles to China and the policy of the parent company in the United States prohibited the Canadian company from following a policy in the interests of our nation. Mr. E. B. Jolliffe, Q.C., a well known lawyer in the city of Toronto-
Mr. Pallet!: A well known C.C.F. lawyer.

A well known C.C.F. lawyer, a very distinguished C.C.F. member-had the opportunity to make a visit to China some time ago and inquiries were made by that

Trade Balance
country about the possibility of obtaining rubber belting in Canada. Mr. Jolliffe came back and, as I recall, interviewed the B. F. Goodrich Rubber Company. The Canadian company said yes they would be very much interested in supplying the belting. Not long after the manager of the Canadian subsidiary wrote to Mr. Jolliffe and said that he was exceedingly sorry, that although they were interested in the sale of rubber belting the policies of their parent company prohibited them from making this sale.

speechtext:
I have not checked the files lately but I do not know what that has to do with my argument. Is my hon. friend questioning the facts in this case? If he is, let him stand up and say so. This man is a very distinguished Canadian. He has put the evidence on the record and it is a shame that industries operating within our nation are not able to conduct themselves in the interests of our country. I think Mr. Jolliffe was acting very much in the capacity of a patriotic Canadian trying to promote Canada's economic interests wherever he went. The government was going to correct our dependence on the United States but there is little sign that this matter has occupied very much of the government's time.
There is a second great danger in allowing more and more of our economy to fall into the hands of foreign investors in that it endangers the degree of prosperity we see about us today in Canada in the event of an impending or forthcoming recession in the United States. With these tremendous obligations abroad, with Canada depending for so much of its prosperity on the inflow of United States capital, any conditions in the United States that may lead to a reduction in such capital coming into our country cannot help but have a very adverse effect on our own well-being.
The influx of United States capital into this country at a tremendous rate has resulted in a substantial premium on the Canadian dollar which in turn has made it more difficult for Canadian export industries to maintain export markets. The Minister of Trade and Commerce seems to consider that this penalty in regard to our export markets is a very modest price to pay for the privilege we have of turning over more and more Canadian industry to outside capital. The government is taking an attitude greatly different from its attitude in former days. We had one speech after another from the Conservative front benches in former days 
criticizing the Liberal administration at a time when there was a large current account deficit. The promise was made that if they formed the government they would do something about it, that they would reverse the dependence of Canada on the United States and take steps to reduce the ownership of Canadian industry by outside capital.
But what has been the result? The result is that everything that the Conservatives used to condemn the Liberal administration for doing or omitting to do is being done or omitted to be done by them on a greater scale than before.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, statistics are available to dispute that statement. I had them here a moment ago. They were taken from one of the government's own publications and from memory they show that, with the exception of the electrical generating industry, the percentage of development by outside capital is increasing. The only mitigating influence is the fact that the electrical generating industry by and large is publicly owned by our provinces and therefore Canadian. But in the manufacturing industry, the mining industry and other industries, more and more of these industries are coming under United States domination because of the mismanagement of the government. How could the facts be otherwise when our deficit is going up at such an astronomical rate? Is it possible to increase our deficit to the United States and to have this tremendous inflow of United States capital without having our industries come more and more under the ownership and domination of outside capital?
The government and' hon. members opposite do not need to take me as an authority on this question. Of course, they will not consider as an authority anybody in Canada who disagrees with them. The annual submission to the government by a man so distinguished and so important as the governor of the Bank of Canada is brushed aside. The Minister of Trade and Commerce took care of the governor of the Bank of Canada the other night in a very sweeping generalization when he said, as found on page 2281 of Hansard:
Taking into account all these factors, the size of Canada's deficit in relation to the foreign earnings capacity, the size of the debt in relation to productive capacity and the trend of consumption and investment in relation to total resources there is little in this picture to substantiate the claim that Canadians have been living beyond their means.

I am very thankful that the governor of the Bank of Canada has been forthright enough to point out the great errors in the policies that this government is following. The governor of the Bank of Canada, I think, is performing a very useful service to the Canadian nation. I believe he is following a very laudable, independent course when he places his views before the government and the country, even though they may differ so greatly from the course now being followed by this government. The governor of the Bank of Canada, in his submission, had this to say in part:
The cumulative effect of all these developments must be to weaken the ability of the Canadian economy to meet the difficulties of the next recession to come upon us from abroad, and to make more likely the development of a domestic recession arising from excesses and structural strains within our own economy which may or may not coincide in timing with recession conditions from abroad.
There is the warning-
Mr. Pallet!: What pages?

The report of the governor of the Bank of Canada, pages 8 and 9. There is the warning of the governor of the Bank of Canada to the minister, that we are not only turning more and more of our economy over to the United States and foreign investors, but the road we are following will eventually lead to a recession in this country because of our vulnerability, brought about by an excessive use of outside capital.
I think it is very good advice. I think it is very sound advice to a country in the stage of economic and industrial development in which Canada is, that we should be generating within our country more and more of the capital we require for expansion. Where could we get this capital? I believe Canadians would be prepared to save more if they were encouraged to do so. I think Canadians would be prepared to save more if they had some assurance that their savings and investments would retain their purchasing power in the years ahead and not be eaten up and eroded by inflation. I think we are in a position to produce more capital by putting idle resources to work. I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce if he does not think that 500,000 unemployed people would be able to produce some of the output, some of the capital requirements for Canadian expansion.
With this tremendous inflow of United States capital, of course, there is a tremendous inflow of goods from the United States. This means that in exchange for the half million Canadians who are unemployed, employment
Trade Balance
in the United States is greater. We are substituting, by reason of this country's dependence to such a large extent upon the inflow of United States capital, jobs for United States citizens for jobs for the half million Canadians who are unemployed. There is a place where the government, by a proper and foresighted policy, could bring about a tremendous increase in Canada's gross national production and, therefore, the opportunity for increased capital within our country.
We heard on former occasions, speeches along the lines of the one I have been making from hon. members opposite when they sat on this side of the house. As a matter of fact one of the proposals that they put before the Canadian people to help bring them to power was the submission that they would take steps to reduce Canada's dependence on the United States; that they would take steps to divert Canada's trade from the United States to other countries; and that, above all, they would take steps to see that Canadian industry was developed in the interests of and in the control of Canadians. The Conservative party put out a very interesting little pamphlet called "Trade", prior to the 1957 election. It was put out by the national headquarters of the Progressive Conservative party and on page 5 we find this:
In 1953 the Liberals promised that they would "use every available means to maintain and expand Canada's external trade and encourage the removal of trade barriers generally."
What we got.
A minus balance of payment of $1,398 million in 1956.
The Conservatives promised the same thing, and what did we get? We got just a little higher minus balance of payments in 1959, namely $1,460 million.
Loss of control of many of our industries to the United States.
We have suffered a further loss of control under this administration in spite of this commitment to the Canadian people.
Tremendous increase in American investment in Canada's natural resources.
This investment has increased In 10 years from $5 billion to $10.3 billion.
I have pointed out how this balance has increased in recent years to over $15 billion and our debt is going up now at the rate of some $125 million a month.
The Canadian economy endangered by making it so dependent upon American prosperity, with no possible alternative.
This was correct when it was stated in 1957, and it is even more correct today than it was at that time.

Trade Balance
Then, on the next page of this pamphlet there is a paragraph headed "Trade", with a subheading "Liberal Failures". Here is what it says:
For generations to come, the benefits of much of our post-war industrial development will accrue to non-resident owners rather than to the Canadians who produce the goods.
This is more true today than in 1957.
Any sudden stoppage of American investment could plunge Canada into a disastrous exchange crisis.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce disagrees with Mr. Coyne today but agreed with him in 1957 when this statement was issued. I know the Minister of Trade and Commerce held a very responsible position in the organizational structure of the Conservative party at that time, and probably had a great deal to do with the issuance of this publication on trade. It goes on to say:
A recession in the United States would reduce the flow of investment capital to Canada, and cause a depression here. The Liberals have not provided any sound alternative to this possibility.
This government has not provided any alternative, sound or otherwise.
No effective action has been taken to protect Canadian exports against the whims of United States tariff policies and practices.
There, Mr. Speaker, is a denunciation of the policies followed by this government, published by the Conservative party, and it might well have been a forecast of the course to be followed by this administration. It is a serious thing when more and more of Canada's wealth is being transferred to foreign ownership. It is a serious thing when we are facing trade difficulties at this time and there must be steps taken to offset these difficulties.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) yesterday presented a subamendment in which were listed a number of points with regard to things we should like to see done. I should like to make some other suggestions and to repeat some of the suggestions that have been made.
I would propose, first of all, that steps should be taken to provide for regulation of prices of key industries by setting up a public tribunal before which companies would have to appear in order to substantiate any increases in prices they might wish to undertake.
The second suggestion I make is that great encouragement should be given to Canadians to save more and to invest more in Canadian industries.
The third suggestion is that Canada should undertake, as we have said in our amendment, a great drive for increased markets and, in order to reduce our trade deficit with the

United States, should be prepared to enter into reciprocal trade contracts with countries willing to purchase increased Canadian exports.
The fourth suggestion I have to make is that we should associate ourselves as quickly as we can with the group of trading nations that have come to be known as the outer seven. We heard yesterday in this debate an attack by the hon. member for York North (Mr. Cathers) on labour in this country and his blaming labour and high wages for making it more difficult for Canada's export markets. I think there are two main reasons that Canadian export industrial industries are coming into difficulty and these are associated together. The first is an inability to adopt modern automation practices to the same extent as have the industries with which they are competing. The second is the fact that Canadian industries do not have access to a very large market and that a market of 17 million people is not enough to provide the kind of efficient production that can be brought about when a larger market is available.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce reviewed very extensively the operations of the inner six and the outer seven; but nowhere was there any indication that this government would adopt a bold policy of associating Canada with the arrangements that have been made for this larger trading area in order to bring the tremendous benefits of a vastly increased consumer market to the industries presently native to Canada; I refer to both manufacturing industries and primary export industries.
Britain made a free trade offer to Canada some time ago and there has been no reply. I think the day has come when Canada should associate itself with the outer seven. I say this because of the advantages I am sure would accrue from such an association. I say it for the further reason that this action would mean at least some transfer of the dependence of Canada today on United States capital and United States investors to an association with nations in northern Europe, namely the outer seven. I am not suggesting by this statement that it might not be advisable to have an even larger trade area. I think that in the days ahead, in this world which is really one world, tremendous progress will be made toward freer trade, the reduction of barriers and the bringing of nations into ever larger and larger trading groups.
The fifth suggestion I have to make is that we should establish in Canada a Canadian investment corporation to obtain domestic capital and, if necessary, to obtain capital

from abroad in order to invest it in Canadian industries. Such a publicly-owned investment corporation would obtain foreign capital on a long term, fixed interest basis, on a basis by which we would amortize the obligation. In my view this procedure would be much preferable to turning over a part of Canadian ownership to outside capital, with all the control and the increase in that ownership that is bound to flow from such a policy. We need increased capital but, in the view of the C.C.F. party, we should be getting a larger and larger part of that increased capital from Canadians; and when we must obtain it from abroad, we should not, if it can be avoided, obtain such capital on an equity basis.
This government's trade policy means a transfer of control over Canada's economic destiny to citizens of other countries. We have a political democracy in Canada. It has been built and improved over the years. We are far away from an economic democracy. As a matter of fact, we are getting closer and closer to an economic dictatorship, with cartels, monopolies and semimonopolies controlled by outside residents. If this economic dictatorship and economic control of Canada's destiny are allowed to continue in their present course we may some day, in the not distant future, find that political control has been removed from our nation and been put into the hands of people living in other countries.
We have seen disturbing trends in that regard in recent days. I mention only the report that the United States atomic energy commission announced that it is going to have a nuclear explosion in the Athabasca tar sands. It was necessary for the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) of this country to deny that any such undertaking could be made by the United States atomic energy commission. But the very fact that they had the temerity to announce that this was to be done shows just how far, in the view of some people in the United States, extends the control of Canada's destiny into their very hands.
I think we are all good Canadians, interested in the building of a prosperous Canada in the control of our own citizens. I commend to the Minister of Trade and Commerce the remarks of his colleagues in former days when they pointed out so vividly and so accurately the dangers of the policies then followed, the dangers of the policies being continued by this government.
