speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been following the debate in this house on this subject with considerable interest, as I think has the whole
Trade Balance
country. Certainly foreign trade is important enough to the people of this country that we must all take it seriously. I think I am speaking accurately when I say we regard even a slight deficit as a problem. It is a problem that I myself, as a member of this house, have been watching with considerable interest. However, I have been struck by the different approaches taken by hon. members who have spoken on this subject.
It seems to me that the best way to handle the problem is to approach it logically. We must analyse the situation, find out where the faults, if any, lie; what is our objective and what are the various methods of attaining the objective which we desire. No one who has been listening to the speeches made in this house can say for one moment that we have heard too little about the problem. This is one aspect of the question which has engaged the entire attention of those members of the opposition who have spoken. We have heard an odd word now and then about the importance of increasing our trade, but certainly the most useful opportunity of the debate, as it would occur to anyone who was anxious to make a helpful contribution, namely the method to be followed, has been almost entirely neglected by the opposition.
I know that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) moved an amendment toward the end of his remarks calling for an Atlantic free trade area. It seems to me that in his quite lengthy speech on the subject he neglected to do something of considerable importance, that is, to tell the house what would be the possible effect of free trade on Canada. The hon. gentleman dealt with the present troubles; he dealt with the problem of trade blocs and so on, but he said nothing about the effect that his amendment might have on any industry in Canada, nor did he seek to explain how it would solve our difficulties.
It is perhaps of significance that there were only 11 Liberal members in the house at the time this amendment was moved. I have observed on earlier occasions that whenever free trade is mentioned a good many hon. members squirm in their seats, particularly those who come from areas where industrial goods, textiles and footwear are produced. Any suggestion of leaving our industry at the mercy of the industrial giants of the south, or of other industrial groups, makes them cry with rage. Perhaps I am being unkind in suggesting that the members who were not present at that time do not agree with the substance of the amendment, but in

Trade Balance
view of the fact that the Leader of the Opposition failed to deal with the possible consequences of the policy he was advocating, the absence of these hon. members provide some grounds for wondering whether the hon. gentleman's suggestion was a political manoeuvre rather than a seriously proposed remedy for some of our economic difficulties.
It might also be unkind to suggest that perhaps the Leader of the Opposition, having made for himself a considerable reputation as a statesman, had formed the opinion that such a manoeuvre might fill in some of the gaps in his reputation as a politician. I do not want the house to think that I suspect he really takes the question as lightly as that, or that the house as a whole should take this problem lightly. The point I am trying to make is that we must assess our difficulties realistically.
One of the prime considerations in ensuring that capital will flow into Canadian enterprises and that Canadian enterprise itself will have confidence in its own destiny, is to make sure that the difficulties and the hardships are not so exaggerated as to be distorted to a degree where they appear insurmountable. In this respect I must say that we have had all too many examples recently of people who have apparently been much more determined to make political capital out of our problems than they were in attempting to reach their solution. Recently I have had a good deal of correspondence from the west. Reports in newspapers noted for their Liberal bias have distorted the facts, for example, about our trade with Japan, suggesting that this government was attempting to slash imports from Japan, with the result that western agriculture would find it impossible to sell any grain to that country. This allegation is so contrary to the facts that I cannot help but feel it shows the complete irresponsibility of some people in their desire to gain a political advantage.
The Leader of the Opposition mentioned the name of Mr. M. W. Sharp, the former deputy minister of trade and commerce, a gentleman who is well known for his Liberal tendencies. Mr. Sharp is one more of those who in speaking of our present trading and financial situation has never failed to exaggerate out of all proportion our present difficulties. I know, also, that another well known Liberal, Mr. Walter Gordon of the Gordon commission, has been making similar statements about the country, exaggerating our difficulties and painting in the blackest possible light both our economic and trading position. This is the gentleman who, as hon.

members will recall, suggested that the solution for the economic difficulties of the mari-times was to evacuate their population because they are not economically able to support themselves. I suggest that those who hold Mr. Gordon in such high regard should convince him that he ought to run for public office, preferably in the maritimes.
As I said, it is of primary importance to take a realistic rather than an exaggerated view of our difficulties. The next important thing is, perhaps, to consider what really is the role of government, what it is that government can really do, bearing in mind that we should like to have a balanced trade and that we should like to see an ever-increasing trade leading to a regularly increasing growth of economic strength. I think many people lose sight of the fact that trade in Canada is not, primarily, a matter of direct government concern. The government of Canada is not a trader; individual companies do their own trading, and as a result the effect which government can have is necessarily restricted to outside or incidental influences.
Having fixed this in our minds, I think we should take a look at the situation today. I do not think enough attention has been given to the fact that we are living in a world which is changing rapidly, and in which the rate of change is increasing from year to year. New countries are coming into existence. These new countries are changing their economic standards. They are developing their own industries to an increasing extent, and the pattern of their demands for goods and services is changing. Similarly, the goods and services which they themselves can provide to the rest of the world, are changing in their nature. In addition, methods of communication and means of transport are changing.
Along with all of this we have the new and growing idea of people who for the first time are becoming educated and changing their demands. We do not have stable governments in every country and their trade policies are subject to change without notice. As a result of all of this I suggest we must take another and closer look at the role government is to play in our trade position. It is not the government but individual manufacturers who are the traders. Therefore the role of the government is to assist and protect them and lend assistance where it can. We must consider both these factors in the light of what changed conditions are going to bring.
I would suggest to my C.C.F. friends that we must recognize the magnitude of the task of gearing the entire production of a country

to the changing concept of world needs which is constantly going on, well knowing the fact that government is usually just a little slower owing to its size and complexity in perhaps appreciating some of these problems. Surely this should be enough to indicate to my socialist friends that the only way you can make a quick change in many fields and among our industries is to make sure that private businesses themselves are given the opportunity to meet each challenge as it arises. I am suggesting that the role of the government is purely advisory in respect to what is necessary for production.
I was glad to hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) give us so much information about the various branches of his department and organizations in the government dedicated to supplying Canadian industry, manufacturers and traders with the latest information as to developments in this field. Certainly the role of any good businessman is to watch all the factors that are going to affect his markets. Each Canadian who owns a firm is certainly going to take advantage of every piece of information that comes his way in order to effectively adopt today a policy for tomorrow, to see if he can determine to the best of his ability what are the factors operating in the foreign country with which he deals that will influence his trading the day after tomorrow. I think we should therefore concentrate on providing information to our businessmen. By "providing" I do not mean that it should be spoon-fed but private enterprise should have ready access to this information in order to increase our trade. We should make sure that the information is efficiently gathered by the government and that it is made available in a form that will make it easy for those interested to consult it.
There is more involved than the provision of information but this is an important undertaking. Before leaving this subject may I advance a suggestion. I believe the government has been doing an excellent job in gathering information and passing it along but in keeping with the increased tempo of foreign competition I believe that some civil servants who are close to the industry should report on it or some who are posted abroad should be brought home to check on what industry is doing in order that the information concerning trade will be even more up to date and useful.
I suppose whenever you are selling there is some risk of not being able to collect. Assistance should be given to other countries so they will have the necessary credit to buy. The government has a most important 79951-0-146
Trade Balance
role to play in making sure that our exporters are not entirely left out of other markets because they are not fortunate enough to be dealing with a country that is part of this or that bloc. I suggest that all these factors taken into consideration are not nearly so important as the initiative taken by the individual exporters themselves. No other single factor contributes so much to increasing sales of our products to other countries than the fact that we can produce the goods more efficiently, more effectively and better than our competitors.
In view of this I think that a certain amount of competition serves a useful purpose and the increased competition we have experienced of late has been a very good thing in that sense. Sloppy business methods should not be allowed to prevail as they have a negative effect on our trading position.
I have sufficient confidence in the skill and ingenuity of Canadian manufacturers to believe that they can and will overcome many of the trading difficulties they are encountering. I suggest, however, that the co-operation of the entire country is necessary. We must have a greater realization on the part of the ordinary working man and investor in this country of the exact difficulties that are being experienced.
Our trading position with Japan will serve as an example. For years the fortunate situation existed in which Canada was able to sell to Japan many times the volume of what that country sold us. The recovery of Japan and her increased productivity as well as her own needs for increased markets has meant that if we wish to continue trading with Japan we must recognize that trade as a two way street. I believe there is a failure on the part of the public to understand that like many other industrial nations Japan has the same facilities for manufacturing as we have. Japan's plants and machinery are every bit as efficient as ours and her businessmen are greatly experienced. In many cases that country does not have the transportation difficulties we have. In addition to that Japanese workers receive considerably smaller wages and so the country can undersell us without difficulty. This has been a cogent factor in our loss of some of our overseas markets. As those hon. members from textile areas in Canada will tell us, Japan has provided rugged competition in our home markets.
In this field I believe the government has acted sensibly. It has refused to be stampeded by the anguished screams of some or the impassioned pleas of others. It might very well have been that some people would have taken advantage of an opportunity of

Trade Balance
this nature to turn the farmer against the manufacturer and vice versa. The government recognized the need of allowing Japan to narrow the gap between us with respect to imports and exports and at the same time sought to encourage sales of our western grains to Japan. I believe the situation has been handled with commendable skill by the government.
The textile industry in Canada has experienced severe difficulty but it is rallying, as private enterprise will, to meet the increased competition. I think there should be a diversification of Japanese exports to this country which would serve to remove the pressure from that particular industry. I think that the people of those industries, in changing their methods, have taken the pressure off this quite a bit and the agricultural community is generally grateful. We are pleased with the part the government has played. I think the general trade situation was unfair and it was only just that we should continue to expand our trade with Japan in a way which has increased the friendly relations between the two countries. It has, I think, served as a model which might well be followed by other industries and by other countries.
I have one more point only. I think we must tell the people of this country that whenever Canadian industry meets competition which they feel is unfair they will be very helpful in helping out Canadian industry by buying more Canadian goods. I do not think it calls for a very great sacrifice most times for the housewife, or the head of the household, to check the product that she is buying, even in instances where it might be a few cents lower in cost, and if at all possible give priority to the Canadian product. I make that suggestion because we are so dependent on a healthy economic situation in the whole country. I think we could make a little more money available generally for investment in Canadian industry if we were even voluntarily to cut down a little on credit buying and thereby make more money available for financing.

I just want to take one or two minutes to add to one point which the last speaker made concerning trade with Japan. It is true that Japan represents an important market for Canadian wheat, and it is important for our prairie provinces and our agricultural industries that that wheat market be extended even at the risk of some interference with our own domestic industries, such as the textile industry and the rubber goods industry. But there is, in my opinion, an even more compelling reason why we should trade

with Japan, and that reason is that we are now engaged in what I think might very well be called a third world war. It is not a shooting war at this point but it is a total war. Unfortunately, trade is one of the very important weapons in this particular war.
Japan is the bastion of democracy such as it exists today in Asia and Japan must trade to survive just as Canada must trade to survive. If Japan does not trade with the western world she will be forced to trade with the communist world, and that would be a disaster for the cause of democracy. It would certainly lead to the domination of Asia by the communist regime because it is communist strategy to make a country dependent upon it, and once that country becomes dependent economically it is a very short step to making it dependent politically as well.
Their strategy, as far as Canada and the United States are concerned, is to take away as many of our markets as possible. They do that by their subsidized loans, by their contracts with clientele nations, and the whole purpose of it is that in time we shall be forced to curtail our production, which will increase our unemployment problem. Because Japan is so important to the free world and so important in this ideological war, regardless of the economics involved it is very important that we see this in its true perspective and do all we can to expand our trade with Japan to keep Japan free and independent of the communist regime.

Mr. Speaker, in every speech the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) makes about trade he always includes a reference to two matters: first, he tries to inject somewhere in his speech something about Tory protectionism; second, he tries to leave the impression that somehow or other the Liberal party is connected with freer trade policies. Both of these references are false. We know it, the people know it and it is about time that he should know it. Yesterday, for example, he spoke of the adjustment on woollen tariffs as being an example of Tory protectionism. He did not, of course, refer to the amount of the increase, for that would have destroyed his argument. The Saskatoon Star-Phoenix, the newspaper which serves my constituency and which follows the line taken by the Leader of the Opposition in this matter, was at least fair enough to refer to the size of the increase as, for example, in the lead editorial of February 23 of this year. In it they quote the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) as pointing out as follows:
They were of a size-

He was referring to the increases.
-not to cut off or divert trade, but simply to allow a number of quite small Canadian woollen mills to keep their heads above water. Many of these mills are located not in big industrial centres but in small towns where little alternative employment is available.
The extent of the tariff increases can be judged from the fact that, according to our computation at the time, the increases might add about 15 cents to the cost of the imported fabrics going into an average suit of clothes, and about 25 cents to the imported fabrics going into an average overcoat. Surely this is not the action of a government bent on high protection.
Although the Star-Phoenix and the Winnipeg Free Press, together with some other persons in the west, have been trying to lead the people of the west to believe that we were restricting trade with Japan, the Star-Phoenix, at least, was fair enough to refer in the editorial to which I have made reference to the fact that in 1954 Canada bought from Japan goods valued at only $19 million; whereas last year we bought from them imports worth $105 million. As everyone knows, the tremendous increase in imports from Japan in 1959 alone amounted to 50 per cent over the 1958 figure. Everyone knows that under a Conservative government we brought about the major part of the increase in imports from Japan and at the same time we have been successful in increasing our exports to them to such an extent that last year we sold them $140 million worth of goods, 50 per cent of which was wheat.
The examples used by the Leader of the Opposition to support his charge of Tory protectionism in fact reflect the determination of this government to increase trade for the benefit of Canadians. The Leader of the Opposition speaks as if he was trying in some way or other to associate the Liberal party with freer trade. Of course, he and other hon. members of this house are well aware of the government's successful efforts to increase our exports, but the Leader of the Opposition, by reference to his proposal for an Atlantic free trade area, once again tried to leave the impression that the Liberal party always strives for freer trade. I think in duty to the truth this bogus argument should be abandoned by him in order that we may get down to the business of seriously discussing methods of further improving Canada's trade relationships on a realistic basis. To clear away some of the debris that clutters up the thinking of the Leader of the Opposition on this problem may I first of all make passing reference to the actual trade situation with Japan. The Minister of Finance, when speaking to the Saskatoon board of trade on February 19 this year, had this to say:
You may be interested in how our actual trade with Japan has developed during the six years 79951-0-146J
Trade Balance
since we signed the trade agreement. In 1954 Japan bought from Canada goods valued at $96 million and sold to Canada $19 million worth, a ratio of five to one in our favour. In each year since then Japan's exports to Canada have increased substantially to an estimated $105 million in 1959. During this period Canada's sales to Japan have also increased, although not nearly as rapidly, and during 1959 we exported to Japan goods valued at approximately $140 million. In the past six years Japan's exports to all countries doubled in value; during the same period Japanese exports to Canada increased sixfold. In the past year alone Japanese sales to Canada rose by some 50 per cent, as compared with a 20 per cent increase in her sales to all countries.
I think hon. members will agree with the Minister of Finance that Japan has done extremely well in extending her sales in the Canadian market. I should like to refer to the terms of entry for Japanese goods. I quote again from the speech of the Minister of Finance:
Japanese goods enjoy freer access to the Canadian market than to the market of any other industrialized country in the world. Apart from moderate tariffs Canada imposes no restrictions of any kind against them. The only special safeguard for Canadian industry rests on a few specific export restraints applied by Japan herself. This is not so in the case of many other countries, including some very rich and powerful countries in western Europe which apply an extensive system of discriminatory import restrictions against Japan, and some of which have refused to extend to Japan the provisions of the GATT.
That is the situation with regard to our trade with Japan. What in fact, is the basic trading position of Canada? We are a nation with a standard of living second only to that of the United States, a nation of only 18 million persons but which is the fourth largest trading nation in the world. We are a nation that is highly industrialized and yet at the same time export chiefly agricultural and primary products, a nation that does more international trade per capita than any other country in the world, a nation that can be damaged more easily from abroad by deviation from what I call fair trading policies than any other nation.
I think the Liberal party propaganda on the trade question is not only deficient in their continual attempt to divide the country into free traders and protectionists, a propaganda line which if it ever did have any validity, that validity certainly lies in the far distant past. Their policy is also deficient in that it does not encompass development and investment policies as well.
There was a time when talk of freer trade did dominate international discussions in his field. Now, I think it is correct to say that a wider, more fundamental approach to the problem of trade is being taken. As I said at

Trade Balance
Washington at the NATO parliamentarians' meeting last November:
-I believe... it is realized that quota tariffs, and even exchange problems, important as they are, are inseparably connected with and cannot be divorced from problems of development, of public and private investment, of technical assistance, of governmental stability, of the maintenance and enforcement of law and order within the nations with which trade in its broader sense is to be conducted and the necessity for the enactment and enforcement of adequate commercial laws.
A proper concept of fair trade policies and fair investment policies is incumbent not only on the Atlantic nations in their relations with one another but as well upon both the less developed nations and the highly industrialized nations of the west in the wider sphere of world trade. Indeed, it is hardly possible to discuss trading policies without bringing within the ambit of that term development and investment policies as well as an integral part of such policy. Fair traders make good neighbours and in this sense of fair trading the special problems of each nation that would be prepared to subscribe to such a concept should be taken into consideration as well as the general principles which may be applicable to the generality of trade and investment.
Before going further into what I conceive to be some of the essentials of fair trading and fair investment policies, I should like to turn for a moment to the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition for an Atlantic free trade area. I gather from the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition that he is not advocating the establishment of such an Atlantic free trade area at this time. In fairness to him I think I should recall to the house that he suggested that it was a matter that should be looked into to see if it had any possibilities and that he was not prepared to say at this time whether or not such a free trade area should be established. In other words, he wishes to dangle the carrot of free trade before the Canadian people without accepting any responsibility for the advocacy of such a development.
It is true that the Leader of the Opposition is not very clear as to what he means by an Atlantic free trade area but I gather he has something in mind like the European free trade area, an area providing for the progressive achievement of free trade through the removal of tariff and other barriers to trade over a certain period, an area with no common tariff around it, an area in which each country would be free to maintain and alter its own tariff and to pursue independent commercial policies. In other words, the area would not be aiming at complete economic integration and there would be no specific [Mr. Jones.}
political objective such as the establishment of an Atlantic community analogous to the European economic community.
Something of the looseness of such an association was indicated by the Leader of the Opposition when I asked him how he thought our trade with Japan would fare if we entered such an association. He replied, if I remember correctly, that each country would be free to maintain and alter its tariff policy with the outside world.
I do not want to go on record as being unalterably, inevitably and irrevocably opposed to such a proposition, but again I think it is necessary to refer to the facts of life in this country in the consideration of such a problem. Europe is a low cost producing area as compared with our own. This may change and I hope it will, but to open our doors now to the widest ranges of low cost European production would inevitably put thousands of Canadians out of work. Nor would we be assured of any compensating advantages to our agricultural exports. At the present time Europe buys from us only what agricultural products they need. They have made special provision in both the common market countries and in the European free trade area for continued protection for the remaining areas of their agricultural economies. It is obvious too from the general pattern of its thinking that the United States would not agree to enter such a free trading area. In other words, we would be associating ourselves almost exclusively with European countries that now take only about 30 per cent of our total exports to the detriment of our trade with those with whom we conduct the balance of our trade.
There is the additional problem of Japan, as I have pointed out. Japan is our second largest customer for wheat. In return for their purchases of wheat and primary products they wish to export to us certain manufactured articles. These articles are in direct competition with European manufactured goods. It would be difficult to reconcile increasing imports from Japan with our obligations to trade with other members of the proposed Atlantic free trade area. This suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition will not meet with much favour in the prairie provinces of our country for it might well destroy our chances for trade with Japan and all that implies in the way of markets for our wheat growers.
As an indication of the concern with which our other trading partners view such a development, may I quote from a report given to this house by the Minister of Finance on January 18 last, when he was relating the developments which had been going on

in Paris in connection with an examination of the possibilities of establishing an organization for Atlantic economic co-operation. At that time he said, as reported at page 26 of Hansard for that date:
Nor were these seven the only countries in the world that were perturbed by the course of events. As the date for Paris drew near the Canadian government received inquiries and representations from a number of other governments, some in the commonwealth and others outside. All of them were worried by the possibility that important movements were on foot, and important decisions were to be taken, in which their interests were involved but in relation to which they had no direct voice. These governments may rest assured that in the recent meetings the Canadian delegation did all that it could, and not without some success, to ensure that their interests were not neglected.
This is an example of the concern of our other trading partners over the arrangements which are going forward at present, let alone the establishment of an Atlantic free trade area. It seems to me that the investigations which are presently being undertaken, as referred to by the Minister of Finance, in the realm of the organization, of trade, and of aid referred to by the minister in that report, are much more likely to result in a sound, realistic expansion of trade, based on mutual co-operation, and supplemented by realistic aid programs to the less developed countries, than any other course presently under discussion. Under such an arrangement, progress toward expanded trade could be made without dislocation of our industries. Our agricultural export market could be maintained and expanded. Our workers will not be thrown out of jobs and private investment abroad may be stimulated in such a way as to bring the greatest returns to Canada if co-operation along the lines indicated by the Minister of Finance at that time comes to fruition.
On this subject of international investment, I should like to refer to an address delivered last December by Lord Shawcross to the royal society of political economy of Belgium in Brussels. It is a very interesting address, particularly in view of the fact that although he had been for six years attorney general of the United Kingdom under the Labour government, he emphasizes the part that private investment can play in supplying the risk capital, administrative and technical skills and progressive entrepreneurship-to use his own words-which is so urgently needed. I quote his remarks here because of their relationship to what has been said by the Leader of Opposition about the dangers of foreign investment in Canada. I also quote them in relationship to the remarks of the hon. member for As-siniboia (Mr. Argue) in order that he may take account of the views of one who has
Trade Balance
held high office in a socialist government. This is what Lord Shawcross had to say:
The fact is that the gains in production that are achieved as a result of foreign investment are accruing increasingly to the benefit of the capital receiving countries.' And more significantly, these gains are being spread widely throughout their economies by generally rising wage standards, growing employment of nationals in managerial, technical and administrative posts, the increasing use of local enterprises for ancillary services and supplies and, of course, the incidence of local taxation. It is, in fact, this very process of disseminating the productive gains from foreign investment throughout the economic system that will inevitably lead to an eventual and steady reduction in the relative share and influence of foreign enterprise in the country's economic activity even if its absolute contribution seems to expand rapidly.
He goes on to say, and I think it is worth while to note:
Once this process has begun to gather momentum, the relative importance and advantage of the foreign sector is eroded away, and even if the foreign enterprises continue to increase in number, their share of the total productive effort will tend to become progressively less significant. In time, as has after all happened in the United States, in Canada and Australia, indeed in the rest of the industrialized world, the distinction between home and foreign interests ceases to matter, although such interests may remain very large, as they do in Canada, in absolute terms. But in spite of the large amount of foreign capital in Canada nobody suggests that Canada is not completely independent both economically and politically.
He has a final remark to make about this general situation which bears very directly on what has been said by those who by their remarks if not by their action would prefer to hinder economic growth in Canada. He says:
No doubt it is not surprising that concern at the size of the foreign sector in the domestic economy should often arise most acutely... at the stage when it is probably about to begin its relative decline. It is often difficult to understand that those very foreign enterprises which seem to be barriers to local progress in fact, partly and often largely, created the conditions which are giving rise to new opportunities for local economic growth, and that if they are allowed to continue to add to the stream of productive experience and opportunity they will, in fact, themselves assist in shifting the balance of economic activity and influence still more toward domestic interests. But so, in fact, it has been in the case of all the industrial countries in which, in the first place, great reliance has had to be placed on foreign capital.
I should like to underline again one sentence from the part I have just quoted. He said:
No doubt it is not surprising that concern at the size of the foreign sector in the domestic economy should often arise most acutely-at the stage when it is probably about to begin its relative decline.
Lord Shawcross is not a person without experience. Although he is out of office, he is not in a position of having dissociated himself from an active study of these problems.

Trade Balance
There is in existence in Europe, created in 1958, an informal committee of international bankers and lawyers who have been investigating some of the problems attendant upon the promotion of international investment. Lord Shawcross in his address also had some interesting remarks to make about the proposal for a multilateral convention to set forth the basic and elementary principles which should be adhered to in order to provide some protection for the international investor. Such a convention is being studied at the present time by the organization for European economic co-operation and was referred to in resolution No. 5 of the economic committee of last November's NATO conference in these words:
Resolved that the NATO parliamentarians' conference endorse the initiative of the O.E.E.C. in undertaking studies concerned with an international convention for the protection of foreign investments to be adhered to by all member countries, and consider such code of declaration to be highly desirable in the encouragement of private investment in the less developed areas, and offers its assistance and co-operation in the promulgation of such a code or declaration.
There we have an example of a proposal for increasing the flow of private investment throughout the trading world. I should like to refer to some of the other resolutions that were dealt with at that meeting last November. However, before I do so, I should like to make one more reference to the subject of private investment in underdeveloped areas. Last June in London I was privileged to submit a paper to the Atlantic congress on the contribution to peace that private enterprise can make in the underdeveloped areas, suggesting that the Atlantic congress consider the adoption of a recommendation directed to the governments of the Atlantic community, requesting them to take appropriate steps to encourage private enterprise in their respective countries, to assist in the development of the underdeveloped countries of the free world to a substantially increased degree, and to this end explore these two possibilities:
1.	The possibility of making available to private enterprise within their respective nations incentives in the form of tax adjustments and of guarantees against non-business risks of investment, of loans and of sales, together with market and other information essential to operation abroad.
2.	Through the good offices of the international bank or in some other suitable collective manner, the possibility of concerting the efforts of the nations of the Atlantic community in this behalf through the establishment of a free world development agency.

I was pleased that when the congress dealt with this matter they adopted a resolution along those lines in these terms:
(e) It will be well for the Atlantic countries to give even more attention than they have in the past to utilizing direct private investment as an instrument for promoting dynamic economic growth in the less developed countries. This is an instrument uniquely at the disposal of the western economies. To this end, we recommend that the highly industrialized, capital generating countries of the Atlantic community should adopt measures that lend encouragement to provide capital flows- through tax concessions, guarantee provisions against non-business risks, through encouraging the establishment abroad of environments compatible to private business operation, and by special efforts to enlist private technical resources in government assistance programs.
Much has been said about our trade with the United States. I myself find it difficult to relate any activities which have taken place in that sphere to any allegations which might have been put forward by the Leader of the Opposition to the effect that Tory protectionism was rampant. I should like to refer to a publication which has, I am sure, reached the desks of all hon. members. It is entitled, "The Growth and Changing Composition of Trade between Canada and the United States" and it is put out by the Canadian-American committee sponsored by the National Planning Association of the United States of America and the Private Planning Association of Canada. On page 6 of that document we read this sentence:
One should add. however, that Canadian restrictions on imports from the United States are now considerably less than they have been in the past.
Whenever these days we hear references made to the subject of Canadian trade with the United States we hear lamentable cries from the opposition about the situation in the uranium industry. Time after time in this house that matter has been dealt with by the government. It has been pointed out that the arrangements that were made with the uranium industry were made by the previous administration and that, in making those arrangements, they did not make adequate provision for safeguarding the substantial investment that was made in those industries in Canada by providing for assured sales past the time at which they have now been terminated. One would think that a person who had been so intimately connected with the previous Liberal administration as to have held the office of minister of public works and who subsequently, upon his involuntary retirement from that office, became president of Rio Tinto, one of the largest uranium producing companies in this country, would know very well the situation in which that industry was based, the historical arrangements which were made for its protection, or the lack of them and that he

would certainly, on assuming his present office, have undertaken immediate steps to provide for alternative markets. What has he done, Mr. Speaker?
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

Before the adjournment I was dealing with some of the references which had been made in regard to the situation in the uranium industry, and I was pointing out that the president of one of the leading uranium producers in this country was the minister of public works in the former Liberal administration. He knew the history of these contracts, he knew the length of time they were to run, and he knew the lack of safeguards there was in those contracts; a serious lack of safeguards, particularly in view of the large investment which had been made in the industry. Yet upon his involuntary retirement from this house when he accepted the presidency of Rio Tinto no steps were taken, as far as I have been able to see, to make provision for the day which would surely come when these contracts would cease. Surely, I say, there is some burden on the trade itself and particularly on the person at the head of such a large company involved, to make provision for its own security. I do not see any record of any strenuous attempts by the industry itself to find alternative uses for uranium.
The hon. member for Assiniboia dealt at some length with what he called the folly of purchasing supplies in the United States. Such a statement must have come as a surprise to hon. members of this house in view of the extensive purchases of supplies and equipment made by the Saskatchewan Power Corporation under the auspices of the C.C.F. government of Saskatchewan; the very course to which the hon. member referred in such disparaging tones this afternoon.
I should like to refer to another practical proposal to assist our trade. I think consideration should be given to increasing the number of trade commissioners and the size of their staffs in order that further encouragement may be given to Canadian exporters. I am sure all hon. members will have noticed with pride the activities of the high commissioner to the United Kingdom as reported in the March 5 issue of the Financial Post where on two full pages of that newspaper are set forth the active co-operation and efficient manner with which our offices in London are assisting Canadian manufacturers to obtain entry into
Trade Balance
the United Kingdom market. Some of the headlines speak for themselves:	"What a
Market Waiting for You in Britain Now!"- "How to Get Rolling in the U.K. Market"- "100 Companies Showing Wares." Another heading says: "U.K. consumers have plenty of cash to spend and they want to spend it on Canadian goods." The article itself is full of praise for the efficient way in which our high commissioner has arranged things in London so that the wares of this country may be brought to the attention of Great Britain. This is another example of the dynamic and progressive policies which this government has been following since it took office in furthering the expansion of our trade on sound and continuing lines.

When the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) delivered his rather lengthy speech on this subject he started off by complaining that he had not been given notice of the intention to raise this question. Despite that he managed to bring into the house with him sufficient statistics to occupy almost three hours of our time with his speech. It is also interesting to note that the minister also brought into this house some persons whom I was very glad to see, namely some of the senior officials of his department. They were in the gallery, and I had the advantage over the minister in that I could sit here and look at them, but he could not.
The measure of the three hours taken by the minister seems to me to be that he devoted no time at all to the subject of the amendment, the demand for a progressive and gradual development of an Atlantic free trade area. Indeed, he seemed to have no ideas on this subject, despite the fact that it is one which has been occupying the attention of several governments in Europe as is evidenced by the trade associations which they have started in the last few years. Perhaps this interest on the part of European governments flows from the fact that those governments have a better and deeper understanding of the necessities of our times than has the minister, and are taking seriously the problems that arise. One is free to adopt whatever conclusion one wishes in the light of the minister's solitary stand.
There is another interesting facet to this problem. The minister appeared to be far too much concerned with proving that the governor of the Bank of Canada was wrong in his statement that we are living beyond our means. There is an interesting matter of policy outstanding here. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) seems at least to be getting credit-wrongly, I often think-for attempting to get the country to try to live

Trade Balance
within its means. If I read his speeches correctly, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, on the other hand, says it is not necessary to do so, and the whole purport of his speech in the course of this debate is in the opposite direction. It could be that everybody else is out of step save the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I wonder about that.
I shall try, however, to direct my remarks in an objective way to the amendment which is before the house and not to scatter bird shot as the Minister of Trade and Commerce did, all to no point. The amendment is:
That all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house expresses its grave concern at the deterioration in Canada's trading position as emphasized by an unfavourable balance of nearly $1.5 billion in Canada's total trade in 1959, and urges the government to deal with this serious problem by taking effective action, including the working out of proposals for the establishment on a gradual and progressive basis of an Atlantic free trade area."
Then there was a subamendment moved by the representative of the C.C.F. group adding a subparagraph as follows:
That the amendment be amended by inserting after the word "including" the letter (a) and by adding to the end of subparagraph (a) and by paragraph (b), to read as follows:
(b) an imaginative and well-planned campaign to expand Canadian exports including:
(i)	use of reciprocal trade contracts with other nations:
(ii)	much greater use of export credit insurance as well as direct federal government credit to foreign buyers;
(iii)	planned reduction of foreign investments in Canada so as to reduce the premium on our currency presently handicapping our export industries;
(iv)	greater economic aid to underdeveloped countries;
(v)	an expanded and intensified effort by the Department of Trade and Commerce to encourage orders for our goods in world markets.
At least the C.C.F. subamendment was directed to the subject before the house, was directly relevant and represented an attempt to deal with the subject. I was a little concerned about the reference to a well planned campaign to expand Canadian exports and by the use of the term "a planned reduction of foreign investments" but it was quite clear from the remarks of hon. members of that group and particularly when their leader was speaking that they did not envisage arbitrary government controls in the use of those words. I therefore interpret the subamendment to mean that these problems concerning the country could be solved by a proper application of proper fiscal financial and trade policies and if I am right in that understanding I do not find anything objectionable in their amendment.
It is to be hoped the government will find nothing objectionable in it.

I am quite aware that you are not getting any leadership in this house from the present government.
The attitude of the government is further illustrated by the fact that in his three-hour talkathon the Minister of Trade and Commerce dealt only with the merchandise trade aspect of the problem. Merchandise trade makes up roughly one third of the total trade of the country. There are other things to indicate the minister's failure to appreciate the problem. I think I could well illustrate his attitude by referring to a question I addressed to him on March 10, 1960 when the daily bulletin of the dominion bureau of statistics first announced this enormous deficit in our total trade. I based my question by reading the first line of the dominion bureau of statistics publication of that day which reported an all-time record deficit for 1959 in Canada's international payments. I described the condition as a serious situation and in reply to my question the minister said, as reported at page 1920 of Hansard of that date:
I do not consider the situation anything like as serious as has been suggested by the hon. member. The daily bulletin has drawn our attention to what it calls a record deficit in 1959 on Canada's international payments.

If the hon. member would reserve his question to the end of my remarks I would be glad to answer. I will not be interrupted now but I will gladly answer his question later.
There are other things that indicate the minister's failure to direct himself to this problem. Since the last speaker referred to uranium I could perhaps select this as an illustration. I shall quote from the minister's speech in which he was talking about the prospects for exports to the United States this year and as reported at page 2295 of yesterday's Hansard he said:
Apart from the problem of lead and zinc Canada's access to United States markets was unaffected by any major adverse developments.
Those words were spoken by the same minister who in answer to an address of this house for the tabling of correspondence with the United States government concerning the extension of uranium contracts tabled two letters, one written in August of last year signed by our charge d'affaires at Washington on the subject of the renewal of uranium contracts and the reply to that signed on behalf of the United States secretary of state. The minister was asked if there was anything more and replied that the government had no more correspondence with the United States government on that subject.

In other words, the minister dismisses the adverse information that uranium, an export to the United States exceeding $300 million a year in value is to be cut off as being of no real significance. Surely that is not the way to treat a problem of this magnitude.
Sometimes it is interesting to do a little research in Hansard. On March 28, 1957, as reported at page 2780 of Hansard, the following exchange occurred between the former minister of trade and commerce, Mr. Howe, and the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) who was then the private hon. member for Prince Albert and leader of the opposition:
In northern Saskatchewan-and I mention this merely as an example-there are available tremendous power resources and mineral resources and the fabulous developments at Uranium city.
Who started those?
Pardon?
Who started the developments at Uranium city?
The people started them and then the government stepped in and took over the paying proposition themselves.

The government started everything in Uranium city. The people were never there.
If the present Prime Minister is of that view on the subject of uranium why does the present Minister of Trade and Commerce dismiss the loss in this field as inconsequential.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What does that prove?

The hon. member for Carle-ton (Mr. Bell) asks what that proves. It indicates that the minister did not direct his attention to the subject matter before the house and does not appreciate the seriousness of the problem. One could find other illustrations in the minister's speech but perhaps 1 have said sufficient to make my point.
The fact is that there is a serious situation for Canada disclosed by the recently published figures of the total trade deficit. Perhaps it would be well to mention some of those factors and bring them into focus before voting this evening. The total trade deficit for 1959 was $1,460 million the largest in our history. But there is more significance to it than that, although that by itself is a fact worthy of the attention of the house. However, let us examine it a little more closely. I now refer to the report of the governor of the Bank of Canada to the Minister of Finance for the year 1959 at page 22.
We find that merchandise trade dropped continuously and very sharply in 1959. The favourable balance of trade on merchandise account with overseas countries which was $474 million in 1955 had declined by 1959 to $132 million. The deficit or unfavourable 79951-0-147
Trade Balance
balance on non-merchandise account with the overseas countries sharply increased. In 1955 the deficit was $137 million; in 1959 it was $356 million. If we take the total balance of trade with overseas countries we see that the figure dropped from 1955 when there was a surplus of $337 million to a deficit last year, the first deficit in a long number of years, of $224 million. Surely the situation revealed by those figures should have been worthy of the attention of the minister. Surely it is a problem that requires our considered attention.
There are some other things that should be said about it. Perhaps I should continue just to point up the problem a bit. The figures just released show some interesting changes. The Minister of Trade and Commerce wished to talk about merchandise trade exports. Let us talk about them. The total in 1959 was up 5.1 per cent over 1958. That is a very good thing; we are all pleased with that. But the minister did not go on and tell us that at the same time the imports on merchandise account increased in 1959 over 1958 by 9 per cent. Perhaps we should break this down a little further just to show some more aspects of the problem. If we take the United States we find that the exports were up 10 per cent. These are things we all appreciate but in addition the other half of the story has to be stated. Imports from that country were up 7.3 per cent. Take the United Kingdom. They talked a lot about the United Kingdom trade. Exports to that country were up 2.1 per cent while the imports from that country were up 13.3 per cent.
Take the other commonwealth countries. Exports in 1959 were down by 2.8 per cent and the imports were up by 14.3 per cent. If you take all other countries you find that in 1959 the exports were up by 5.2 per cent and the imports were up by 11.6 per cent over 1958. Surely those figures create a problem for Canada, a serious problem, that must receive our careful attention. When I am giving these figures I wish hon. members opposite would realize, if they follow the statistical information carefully, that in addition to the figures which I have given in terms of current dollars, our exports were up in price and our imports were down in price a little, so that the picture is even worse than the figures I have indicated, if you make that slight adjustment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: The hon. member means we are selling for more and buying for less. Is that bad business?

The explanation is quite simple; the volume of imports was increasing, as will be found when I continue with my argument a bit farther.

Trade Balance
Let us examine the nature of those imports; what is the kind of import? Yesterday afternoon the Minister of Trade and Commerce interrupted the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) when he was speaking, and again in his own remarks he referred to the situation in 1956 when a problem similar to this was causing concern to the government of that day. But the difference is very interesting. The government of that day took some action about it; the government of that day was operating with a surplus, a thing unheard of in these days. It is rather interesting to know that the cash surplus in 1956-57, the year which the minister was criticizing, was $940.6 million. This is the thing we are complaining of now, this spendthrift government and particularly the portfolio under the irresponsible administration of the Minister of Finance who seems to have lost his sense of responsibility in certain expenditures he makes-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: You have lost your sense of responsibility.
I am prepared to back that statement up, if you wish me to.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: There is no foundation for it at all.

Since taking over the minister has had a deficit of something over $2 billion, which I am quite sure no supporter of the government should be proud of; and when you bear in mind that that deficit was composed in large part of utterly useless expenditures improperly made by the Minister of Finance, then you can-
Increases in old age pensions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: You did not vote against any of them.

-see how serious it is.
There is one other thing about the difference between 1956 and 1959, and that is the question of the content of the imports. The imports in 1956 had a much smaller percentage of consumer goods among them than the imports in 1959. The imports in 1956, when the government of the day was concerned with this problem, had a much larger content of capital goods used in production and the development of resources and for the creation of assets that would produce wealth. What is happening now is that the imports are in the consumer goods field; the consumer imports are sharply up. The latest figures I could get-I could only get them this afternoon-cover comparative figures, taking the first nine months of 1959 and the corresponding nine months period for 1956. Anyone examining them will find that the

percentage of consumer goods in relation to total merchandise imports is up by 15 per cent. He will find that investment goods are down 6.3 per cent, and industrial materials are down by 4.4 per cent. This is the trend under this government's direction. Then, of course, all industrial materials and investment goods are not all capital goods that create wealth; capital goods that are used in the development of our resources for the creation of development are to be found in those items, so that the situation is surely pretty serious if viewed in the light of those statistics.
Hon. members opposite seem to think very little of this problem. They think the $2 billion deficit of their Minister of Finance-I regret he is not in his seat; I would like to say something about some of those expenditures-is a joke.
Talk about the assistance to the farmers. Talk about the increase in old age pensions. Talk about all the other things.

Yes, I will talk about them. I think the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) should be told some of the facts of life. It is about time he was. You see, Mr. Speaker, in his interjection the Postmaster General did not tell us about the $20,000 that he as a minister of the crown approved being remitted to a Vancouver citizen in August of last year. If he will read Hansard of a few days ago he will find that when bail was forfeited in a narcotics case in 1956 an application was made to a judge of the court for relief against forfeiture-

Mr. Speaker, I am seeking to come directly to the subject matter under discussion. We are discussing the balance of trade and in doing that it is absolutely necessary to show wherein the danger lies in the large deficit figure. One of the dangers is that this kind of problem may be handled when there is a balanced budget or a surplus but it cannot be handled when the country is running into huge deficits which among other things add to costs of exports. That is the purport of my argument.

There have been such irresponsible actions as that by the Minister of Finance in his conversion loan when he wrongly included the ninth victory loan which resulted in imposing an utterly useless charge of $165 million on the Canadian people over the period from 1958 to 1965. If the ministers want some more information it will be given to them.
There is another facet of this problem. The total of interest and dividend payments by Canada to other countries rose to $656 million in 1959, higher than ever before. That is particularly important when we remember that in addition to what I have said about the content of our merchandise imports borrowings, as was so ably set out by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Dumas), by Canadians in the United States, which make up the larger part of the balance of payments, now consist of a substantial volume of bonds issued by provincial and municipal governments for purely service purposes within the responsibility of those governments and not for the creation of production and wealth in this country. We must also remember that all too many of our service industries are borrowing in that country for services as opposed to the development of resources. I am not going to deal with that subject fully because I do not have adequate time to do so but if hon. members care to read more on the subject they will find that there has been a rather interesting debate in the other place which will give them plenty of ammunition.
Mr. Pallet!: So that is where you are getting your material?

There is also a contribution to the bad situation with respect to our total trade by the failure of the government since it took office to deal with our oil and gas policy. The government delayed two whole years before setting up an energy board. Then we debated that subject in the house and at that time we were led to believe by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that they would immediately appoint a board so that it could get on with what was considered to be urgent and important business, and I think 79951-0-147J

it was important and urgent business. How much delay was there before the board was appointed? Hon. members will recall that it was many months before these matters were dealt with.
You have shown so much knowledge about oil and gas-

I will let the record speak for itself. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) is just not speaking factually when he makes that interjection. If he knew anything about the industry he would know how costly that delay has been, how adversely it has affected our total trade balance with the United States and he would also know something that is more important to his own constituency, how it has hurt the city of Edmonton.
There was another interesting facet of the debate and that was the complete absence of anything from the Minister of Trade and Commerce on the subject of the movement toward free trade in the Atlantic area. In addition, when he mentioned the European common market and the European free trade association he did not go any further than to make a few general remarks about them. But he left one very outstanding matter totally neglected. When he dealt with the meeting at Mont Tremblant two years ago preceding the commonwealth economic conference, which the government took so much credit for calling, he did not remind the house that the United Kingdom representative made an offer to this country of free trade. He did not tell the house that the government did not consider that problem and that they did not bring it up at the ministers' conference in Montreal. He did not tell the house that when the minister from the United Kingdom was here a few weeks ago he indicated that he was still ready and willing to discuss that subject. He did not tell the house that the government still would not consider it, that they brushed it aside.
He did not mention the cavalier disregard of such an important subject matter by the government, the failure to explore the possibilities to see whether there was anything in the proposal, to see exactly what was meant by it, to see whether what was proposed would be beneficial to Canada. He also did not tell us what effect the failure to do that had on the position of the British with respect to the European trade blocs that are being formed. He did not tell us what position the attitude of the government put the British in with relation to their bargaining with the free trade association, their bargaining with the-

Then there is another interesting thing. He talked about trade with Japan. I do not know whether the remarks of the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Jones) were intended to be a supplement to those of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. As I understood the hon. member for Saskatoon, he was seeking to say that any movement toward improving our trade relations with the European area would adversely affect our trade with Japan. On a point of order, that is not what I said at all.

If that was the purport of his argument, I can only differ with it. I may not have understood him correctly, but I would say that the strengthening of our trade relations, where we are rapidly losing our trading position in the European area, would only better our chances for trade with Japan and improve our trading position with Japan. I am sure that every western farmer wants our trade with Japan to be improved because it is an outstanding actual and potential market for our grain products. It is for this reason that during the last two years I have been continually at the ministers on that very point.
Incidentally, the hon. member for Saskatoon went on to quote some remarks made by Lord Shawcross, and I take it he quoted them with approval. Those were intended to show that foreign investment was not a bad thing. I have no quarrel with the remarks, but the hon. member must have misread them completely. If he will look at the first of those remarks he will see they are predicated upon foreign investment for the creation of production facilities, the very point we are talking about, and the very point we say constitutes the difference between the situation in 1956 and in 1959 when foreign goods that are coming into Canada are consumer goods and the foreign investment is for things that do not create wealth. The hon. member will see that error if he studies the statistics. He will see how far astray he has gone, and he will see further that the remarks of Lord Shawcross which he has quoted with approval, and which were rather interesting, were in support of the position we have been taking yesterday and today. He will see the distinction drawn throughout the whole of the remarks concerns foreign capital for the production

of wealth as opposed to the import of foreign capital to pay for luxury merchandise and to pay for services to the population. He will see that distinction made all the way through.
I make no apology for taking the time of the house to deal with this subject. I consider this one of the major problems facing Canada today. It affects the whole problem of our trade and our whole economic future. There is a material worsening in our position, as the figures have shown. I should have thought, and I would have hoped, that the government would have dealt with it in a responsible way rather than leaving two thirds of the problem not dealt with at all and the other one third dealt with in a wholly inadequate way. If these problems are big, and they are big, here was a motion that put them before the house for debate. I am unable to hear precisely what the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) is saying, but there is no mistaking the tone of his voice which, perhaps, indicates the peculiar substance of his thought.

Mr. Speaker, my first words with reference to this motion must be words of congratulation to the minister upon his careful review of matters of trade and commerce. I think I can speak for the people of western Canada when I say we would rather listen to the optimism of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) than the gloom of the opposition. In fact, I think I can speak for the people of western Canada when I say that we would rather listen to the optimism of the Minister of Trade and Commerce than to the statements made by Mr. Coyne that we have to tighten our belts and things are not so good in Canada. It is the confidence that you have in business that builds business in Canada.
In the few moments I have left to make any remarks on the motion itself I should like to say a few words with regard to wheat and coal. When this government took over we inherited one of the largest surpluses of

wheat ever piled up in Canada. This government went to work and in the first year we sold more wheat, to the extent of $22 million, than had been sold on any other occasion in Canada. The second largest purchaser in the world of our grain is Japan. Last year I had the opportunity of being in Japan and I am happy to note that we are encouraging trade relations with that country. Not only is Japan buying our grain, but she is also buying our western coal.
When I accepted the nomination in the constituency of Bow River, 80 per cent of the working force in places like Canmore and Drumheller were unemployed. Today, because of the subventions on coal put on by this government and because of the type of sales that have been put forward by this government, I can safely say that in the town of Canmore, which has a population of about 1,500 there is full employment.
In the few moments I have left, I want to speak on another matter which concerns everybody in the province of Alberta and everybody in western Canada. I refer to the export of our natural gas. I notice that on page 2265 of Hansard the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) criticized the government for delay in the export of natural gas from Alberta. I should like the Leader of the Opposition to get in touch with the former leaders of the Liberal party in Alberta. For years the Liberal record has been very clear in that province, and without exception they have opposed the export of any gas from Alberta. First, we had Mr. Prowse, who led the Liberal party from 1953 to 1957. He was opposed to the export of gas and spoke along that line in the legislature. Then, we had Grant MacEwen, the new leader who was defeated in the last election. He opposed any export of gas from the province of Alberta. Then, we had one of the top spokesmen for the Liberal party, Mr. John Macdonald, who was the senior member of the legislature, and he opposed the export of natural gas from Alberta.
When the Leader of the Opposition says to this house that this government is responsible for delay, let me ask him about his party. Do they say one thing in the province of Alberta and another thing in other parts of Canada? They are on the record. The indictment is against' the Liberal party in the province of Alberta for opposing the export of natural gas. When this government took over there was no medium set up to take care of this problem. This government, therefore, immediately stepped into the breach and set up a royal commission to ascertain what the proved reserves were. Unless we have ascertained the facts, we cannot make decisions.
Division
No members can come up with a decisive factor unless they have the evidence before them. This government immediately stepped into the breach and set up a royal commission. From that royal commission was set up the energy board. The energy board now is set up in such a fashion that we have before the energy board facts as to our proved reserves. We in the province of Alberta now know that we have 23 trillion cubic feet of gas, and probably 27 trillion. We know we have reserves of approximately 300 trillion feet of gas that may and can be discovered in the future. On those facts that board can base a sound judgment. That has been done by this government.

Mr. Speaker, my grievance is that the Hutterite farms in western Canada are not subject to income tax in the same manner as are all other farmers in western Canada. I raise this question very seriously because the Hutterite problem is becoming more pronounced in western Canada. No member in this house from western Canada will question my saying this. In the past dozen years there have been at least half a dozen commissions set up to study this question in the three prairie provinces. I want
Non-payment of Income Tax by Hutterites to make myself abundantly clear by saying that I have no grudge whatsoever against these people. I feel that they are in a sense receiving a subsidy from all the rest of the taxpayers in Canada and that is my only grievance.
I should point out, Mr. Speaker, that the Hutterites as individuals are subject to income tax, but that the colony in which all the property is held is not. The individuals do not receive high enough salaries, they do not receive any dividends from the colony, and therefore it is very doubtful whether they have ever been in receipt of a taxable income.
I should like to point out that these people are very good farmers. I have nothing against their mode of farming. They have excelled and are considered authorities on the question of farming. My main objection is that they are receiving a definite advantage over all other farmers in western Canada. I raise this point at this time partly because of recent action on the part of the Alberta government.
I mentioned a while ago that there have been numerous studies in the three prairie provinces concerning this problem. In those studies-and I have copies of them before me -at all times in Manitoba and Saskatchewan they point to the communal properties act of Alberta and suggest that the use of this act is perhaps one method to control the acquisition of land by those Hutterites; but recent action by the Alberta government in amending this act has thrown it wide open. Mr. Taylor, the minister of highways in Alberta states- and I am reading from the Gazette of Tuesday, March 22-that the government in Alberta is not going soft on the Hutterites. He made this quite clear. Then he goes on a little later to say that the whole purpose of the amendment to the act is to leave the decision as to where they should acquire land to the cabinet. The people in my constituency certainly know what this means.
Two years ago the Hutterites attempted to purchase a large tract of land in my constituency. I might say that this tract of land is the largest consolidated, deeded acreage in Canada. It is commonly known as the V-Bar-V ranch, which was set up under the Credit Foncier mortgage company. They tried to buy this land, which was directly contrary to the communal properties act in Alberta. The ranchers and the neighbouring farmers threatened to sue the Alberta government, and the Alberta government rescinded their order in council allowing the Hutterites to move in there, and gave the Hutterites two weeks to move off the V-Bar-V ranch.
I might say that those who were promoting the sale stood to make over $1 million profit on the sale of this land to the Hutterites. Surely hon. members can realize
