Non-payment of Income Tax by Hutterites what effect this new amendment is going to have. It is going to allow the cabinet to decide where these people will move and whether the move is advisable. There is going to be no regulation of such movement whatsoever. I definitely feel that this is a retroactive step on the part of the Alberta government. I definitely feel that they are going soft on the Hutterites, and I am certain this can be well borne out by the fact that the rural municipalities association of Saskatchewan suggested in 1956 that the Saskatchewan government adopt similar legislation to the communal properties act. As for Manitoba, at one time there was a gentlemen's agreement between the municipalities and the Hutterites as to a similar regulation.
This is one of the things that prompted me to raise this grievance at this time. As I pointed out, the Hutterites are exempt from income tax under section 62 (1) (e) of the Income Tax Act which reads as follows:
A charitable organization, whether or not incorporated, all the resources of which were devoted to charitable activities carried on by the organization itself and no part of the income of which was payable to, or was otherwise available for the personal benefit of, any proprietor, member or shareholder thereof.
Certainly I have no objection whatsoever to their religious beliefs. I feel strongly that anybody should be able to worship according to his beliefs, but certainly their farming should not be considered as part of their religion. The neighbouring colony in my constituency operates a farm of approximately 22,000 acres. I am certain that all members will fully realize the size of some of these enterprises. I should like to quote from a case that went to the supreme court in which Mr. Justice Rand stated that a religious society may or may not be a charitable society. He cited the case of Cocks vs. Manners. I might say that this case arose out of the assessment of a religious organization which was operating a dry cleaning business. Mr. Justice Rand stated:
The question in controversy involves the characterization given to the corporation and its activities. A charity or charitable society is, I should say, one whose purposes are those described in the preamble-
He goes on to say:
They can be classified generally, as for the advancement of religion, for the relief of poverty, for the promotion of education, and for other purposes bearing a public interest; and the attributes attaching to all are their voluntariness and, directly or indirectly, their reflex on public welfare.
I have not got the time tonight to go into the effect of these societies on public welfare but any western member will fully realize what these societies will do to a community.


I should like to quote what the English law dictionary in the library says concerning charitable organizations. It is one which has no capital stocks, no provision for making dividends and profits but derives its funds mainly from public and private charity. I looked up the word "charity" in the same law dictionary and I find that the word "charity" comprises four principal divisions; the relief of poverty, the advancement of religion, the advancement of education and other purposes beneficial to the community.
In considering these four things it can be said that these people are only trying to relieve the poverty of their children and certainly every member of the house is doing the same thing. But these people contribute very little, if anything, to the general relief of poverty and to the well-being of the community as a whole. As for the advancement of religion, certainly they do not go out and try to impose their religion upon others but they do carry on religious worship in their own community and I have no objection whatsoever to that.
As for the advancement of education, the Alberta royal commission set up to study the Hutterite question found that they were actually retarding education. Of 923 pupils studying in Hutterite schools in Alberta, 699 were considered to be behind in their grades and to be retarded pupils. Out of 923 over two thirds were behind in their grades and were considered retarded pupils. The Alberta commission considered that 216 out of the 923 were average students and only 8 out of the 923 were considered to be accelerated pupils. When we compare this with pupils in the other schools of Alberta we find that in those schools 35 per cent are to be considered to be behind in their grades, 45 per cent are average and 19.61 per cent are considered to be accelerated pupils. This latter figure compares with only 8 of 923 Hutterite pupils. Therefore I think it is abundantly clear that they are not advancing education.
As for the question of other purposes beneficial to the community, they carry on their own business, buy all their goods wholesale and contribute very little to the community. As I said before, I have not got all the time I should like to have in order to go into how these people actually live. It is hard to describe. It would take a great deal of time to do it well because it is hard for a person who has never seen a Hutterite farm to visualize how they live and what their standard of living is. I say that in all sincerity. I am certain that other western members who are familiar with the Hutterite farms know exactly what I mean.

On the same question of the definition of a charity or charitable organization I have 1929 Appeal Cases here and I should like to refer to a case that went to the privy council. The case originated in Australia but it has some bearing in that it describes a public charitable institution and it says:
-an institution which, assuming its public character ... is charitable in the sense oi affording relief to persons In necessitous or helpless circumstances.
As I pointed out, these people afford charity to themselves only and certainly they cannot be considered to be in helpless or necessitous circumstances. In the past years there has been a rapid growth in the number of Hutterites and Hutterite colonies in Alberta. The growth in population in the Hutterite colonies in Alberta between 1951 and 1956 was 19.8 per cent. This percentage was equal to the growth in population in the province itself, but of course the province received a large number of immigrants from other countries and people from other provinces, whereas the Hutterite growth was a natural growth within the colonies.
I have the figures here for the province of Manitoba and in that province the population increase from 1951 to 1956 was nearly 25 per cent. The acreage that they control in Alberta is close to 500,000 acres. I do not have exact figures as to the acreage they control in the other western provinces. They have been migrating from Alberta into Saskatchewan in recent years because of the communal properties act in Alberta.
An interesting point concerning income taxes is made in the Alberta report on page 11 where it is stated that at one time they were assessed and the elders journeyed to Ottawa and presented their case. Subsequently, unlike any other partnership, the profits are theoretically divided equally amongst the members for the purpose of taxation. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that nowhere else is a farmer with half a dozen sons allowed to theoretically divide his profits so that he may not pay income tax.
There was a case in Saskatchewan about 1945, just as I was leaving Saskatchewan, which involved a farmer who had a great number of sons. He had a large amount of land which he had kept in his own name and the government was taking a net worth statement from him for income tax purposes. He could not theoretically divide this property amongst his sons. He was told either to divide it or they would tax him accordingly. The government of that day taxed him accordingly and the outcome of the case was that this early pioneer farmer hanged himself because of the action taken to collect income taxes.
Non-payment of Income Tax by Hutterites
This business of allowing a company or a corporation to theoretically divide the profits for taxation purposes is something that applies to no other company or corporation. Any company could, theoretically, divide its profits and thereby reduce the amount of income taxes that would be paid by any member of the corporation because each member would be in a lower bracket than if the profits were left in the hands of the corporation. If this statement in the Alberta government report is true, then certainly that principle is wrong. The Hutterites should not have any privilege so far as the farm corporation is concerned to theoretically divide their profits. On page 16 of the same report it says:
Somewhat later the colony secured control of extra land or territories within 40 miles of the existing colonies by providing some of their members with funds from the colony treasury to purchase land as individuals and not as trustees or agents of the colony. This is how they would start another colony.
In my opinion, this is a direct violation of the Income Tax Act which says: no part of the income which was payable to or which was otherwise available for the personal benefit of any property member or shareholder thereof. This is a loophole that they found in the communal properties act and it results in a direct violation of section 62 of the Income Tax Act, so there should be no doubt in the mind of anyone that they could be assessed for the money they spent in buying extra property.
This same question was raised in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix this year. On February 17 one of a series of four articles on the Hutterite question in Canada appeared in that newspaper. It was stated there that individual Hutterian land-owners or elders may have purchased land in Alberta in their own names and may not have considered the Department of National Revenue in their dealings. There is, therefore, a great deal of question as to whether or not this is possible.
I should like to deal for a minute with the question of the Hutterite farms in its entirety and whether or not the sect and their farms come within the definition of a religious organization. The citation I should like to read to the house is from the case of The King v. Assessors of the Town of Sunny Brae. This case arose in the province of New Brunswick and I quote from the maritime provinces reports, 1951. This is the decision of the court of appeal and the court held that the religious organization, the English name of which was the Home of the Good Shepherd, was taxable because it was considered they were carrying on a business. The town, therefore, had every right to assess them to the value of the business, the value

Non-payment of Income Tax by Hutterites of the property they used in that business. Mr. Justice Richards had this to say:
If the work in question were restricted to that required for the officials, employees or inmates of the institution, no question would arise, but when the work becomes a business in competition with general public business, then the property employed should be subject to taxation in the usual way.
Then I go to the judgment of Mr. Justice Harrison, and I quote:
If this laundry and dry cleaning business were operated merely to do washing and cleaning for the inmates of the institution, then the equipment would be used as part of the charitable undertaking of the society. The equipment in the case before us is used in the operation of a laundry and dry cleaning business which gets customers who would otherwise have their work done by taxpayers. To exempt such a business from taxation would be contrary to the intention of the act as it would be an unjust discrimination against others carrying on laundry and dry cleaning business and paying taxes upon all property and equipment used in such business. To exempt a competitor such as this society would, in effect, be a forced levy on the other taxpayers. It would amount to a subsidy to one competitor in the laundry and drycleaning business which would have to be paid by other taxpayers.
I hold that the Hutterite case bears a great deal of similarity to this case. We farmers of western Canada are, in effect, subsidizing one of our largest competitors. These Hutterite farmers go to the auction sales, the cattle sales and compete against other farmers. They have the same freedom as any other farmer. They buy machinery and repairs in the same manner and they put their produce on the market in the same manner as any other farmer does.
In support of the argument that they are farmers I should like to read another case that came to the courts in 1939. I am reading from the Canada Supreme Court Reports. This was a case concerning a Hutterite corporation, as to whether or not they were farmers under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act of 1934 and the amendments thereto. The Supreme Court of Canada held that the corporation was a farmer within the meaning of that word used in the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement act of Manitoba of 1934 and the amendments in 1953 and was entitled to take advantage of that act.
This points out again, Mr. Speaker, that they are considered in every light to be farmers. There are, I might say, some definite differences in connection with this farm organization I might point out to those who are afraid that I might be going out to tax every religious corporation. I have no such thought in mind and I wish to assure the house that I have no such thought in mind. They have six main differences-I refer to this corporation-as compared with the others.

In 1958 when this government paid acreage payments to western farmers the Hutterites received their acreage payments. They have permit books. They sell grain in the same manner as does any other farmer. They collect the baby bonus if they fill out the forms. They receive deficiency payments for wool; in every case if they sell wool they will receive deficiency payments from this government. They pay taxes on their land. They pay municipal taxes on the land they farm. They pay municipal taxes on the land on which their buildings are situated. This is a decided difference from anything else in Canada. Then there is another point. They take out no citizenship in any country. They do not want to do so. They declare themselves to be noncitizens of Canada. They will not take out citizenship papers in this or any other country. This is a decided difference from anything else we might have in Canada.
In western Canada right now we have the three prairie provinces all setting up farm loan boards in order to lend money to farmers to purchase land. The Hutterites are the only farmers in western Canada who have any money with which to go out and buy land. It has come down to that point. The banks are out of the business as far as the lending of money is concerned to purchase land. The banks very rarely go into this business any more. The government loan board is the only place to which the farmer can turn. The Hutterites in most cases are able to use their own resources and reserves because one colony aids another in the same manner.
I made some inquiries as to how the Hutterites were taxed in the United States and what laws existed concerning them there. In South Dakota there is a law prohibiting Hutterites from forming any more colonies in that state. I was told that the Hutterites pay income tax similar to corporations and co-operatives down there and that they receive the same treatment as do those cooperatives and corporations down there.
I solemnly urge this government to take a close look at this problem. I urge the government to try to envision the prairies 50 years or 100 years from now if this situation continues. I say this in all seriousness because their rate of growth is great. A few years ago there were few Hutterites in the province of Alberta. Today they are spreading fast into Saskatchewan. If a line is drawn across the map of Alberta at Edmonton, from that line south to the United States border there is no other spot at which a Hutterite colony could be established without breaking the communal properties act which states that Hutterite colonies shall be

40 miles apart. That is the situation from Edmonton south to the border. When they were told they had to go up north to the Peace river they said no, that they did not want to do that. They did not want to explore and develop the country. This matter they leave to the pioneers. They were not pioneers. They told the Alberta government that this was their policy. They wanted to live near a community so that they could peddle their eggs, potatoes and vegetables to that community.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker and to all other hon. members that this problem should be seriously considered. Hon. members should try to envision the picture in the prairie provinces 100 years from now if these people are allowed to go on earning money untaxed and purchasing more and more land. For those in the colony this is their main purpose. The main revenue they receive from the sale of their produce is directed into the purchase of more land. As soon as a colony reaches a total of about 100 persons they immediately look for new land and swarm like a flock of bees to settle in another spot. Just try to picture the prairies 100 years from now if these people are allowed to go untaxed.
I hope that this government can cover all the problems that may have to be faced and that stand in the way so that these farmers can be treated in the same manner as are all the other farmers in western Canada and be subject to a net worth statement in the same manner as are other western farmers in western Canada today.
Mr. Speaker, I intend to be only a minute or two.
Ten o'clock.
If the house will not grant me that minute or two-
Go ahead.
I regret very deeply this most unwarranted attack on one of the most harmless minorities, if not the most harmless one that exists in Canada.
